title: Photosynthesis: how leaves make food from air, water and light

summary.text: A huge tree grows from a small seed, yet the soil they grow in hardly gets lighter. Most of the tree is built from the air. Green leaves take in carbon dioxide, a gas in the air, and water from the roots. They use the energy of sunlight to join them into sugar. This is called photosynthesis. Oxygen is left over and goes out into the air. The plant builds their whole body from that sugar, and almost every food we eat began this way. Scientists know the main steps well. Some details, like how a leaf moves the energy of light so quickly, are still being worked out.
summary.art: A neem tree in sunshine with arrows: sunlight arriving from the Sun, an invisible puff of air going into a leaf, water rising from the roots, and tiny bubbles of oxygen floating out to a child breathing in.

intro.hook: Pick up a mango stone. This seed fits in your palm, yet the mango tree they grow into can weigh more than a lorry. Where does all that tree come from?
intro.text: Most people, even most grown-ups, guess the soil. That seems obvious, because a plant sits in soil all their life. Nearly 400 years ago, Jan Baptist van Helmont, a doctor in what is now Belgium, tested that guess. He dried and weighed a big pot of soil. He planted a small willow tree in it and gave the tree only rainwater for five years. Then he weighed everything again. The tree had gained about 75 kilograms. The soil had lost only about 60 grams. So the tree did not come from the soil. In this unit, you will find out where the tree did come from.
intro.art: A child holding a small mango seed in an open palm, with a huge mango tree towering behind, and a question mark drawn in the air between them.

outcomes: I can say what photosynthesis is: green leaves make sugar from sunlight, water and carbon dioxide, and give out oxygen.
I can run a fair test that shows a leaf needs light and carbon dioxide to make food. I can show my results in a table and a chart.
I can test a food or a leaf for starch with iodine, and explain what the blue-black colour means.
I can explain, with evidence, that a tree is built mostly out of air.
I can explain why leaves are green, and what chlorophyll does with sunlight.
I can explain that plants also use up food and oxygen, and that nearly every food chain starts with photosynthesis.
I can say what scientists agree about, who found it out, and what is still unknown. I can also follow the idea out to atoms, the Sun and the history of Earth's air.

terms.meaning: How green plants make their own food. They use the energy of light to join carbon dioxide and water into sugar. The word means 'putting together with light'.
terms.example: Every green leaf on a tulsi plant is doing photosynthesis while the sun shines on it.
terms.art: A leaf in sunlight with three arrows going in (light, air, water) and two coming out (sugar staying in the leaf, oxygen bubbles leaving).

terms.meaning: The flat, usually green part of a plant. Most of a plant's food is made inside their leaves.
terms.example: A banana leaf, a neem leaf and a blade of grass are all leaves.
terms.art: Three different leaves side by side: a wide banana leaf, a small toothed neem leaf, a thin grass blade.

terms.meaning: A gas in the air. You cannot see it or smell it. You breathe it out every time you breathe. Plants take it in through their leaves.
terms.example: Every time you breathe out, you send carbon dioxide into the air. A leaf nearby can take it in.
terms.art: A child breathing out, with faint dotted puffs drifting towards a leaf.

terms.meaning: A gas in the air that people and animals need to breathe. Leaves give it out while they make food.
terms.example: Water plants in a pond give off tiny bubbles of oxygen on a sunny day.
terms.art: A water plant in a glass with a stream of tiny silver bubbles rising.

terms.meaning: The food a leaf makes. One sugar that leaves make is called glucose. The sugar in your kitchen is another sugar made by plants, in sugarcane. All sugars store energy.
terms.example: Sugarcane stores so much of their sugar in their stem that we squeeze it out as juice.
terms.art: A sugarcane stalk being pressed in a roadside juice machine, a glass of green-gold juice beside it.

terms.meaning: A store of food that plants make by joining lots of sugars together, like beads on a long string. Rice, potatoes and wheat are full of it.
terms.example: When you cook rice, the soft white part is mostly starch made by the rice plant's leaves.
terms.art: A plate of rice, a potato and a roti, with a zoom showing chains of tiny sugar beads.

terms.meaning: A way to find starch. Brown iodine turns blue-black when it touches starch.
terms.example: A drop of iodine on a slice of potato turns blue-black. On sugar or salt it stays brown.
terms.art: A potato slice with a blue-black spot and a spoon of sugar with a brown spot, an iodine dropper above.

terms.meaning: The green colouring in leaves. It catches the energy in sunlight. It soaks up red and blue light and bounces green light back, so leaves look green.
terms.example: Grass is green because of chlorophyll.
terms.art: Sunlight split into a rainbow hitting a leaf, the red and blue going in, the green bouncing back to an eye.

terms.meaning: A tiny green bean-shaped part inside a leaf's cells. It is where photosynthesis happens. One leaf has many millions of them.
terms.example: Under a strong microscope, a cell from a moss leaf looks like a box full of green beads. Each bead is a chloroplast.
terms.art: A microscope view of leaf cells like rooms, each packed with small green ovals.

terms.meaning: Tiny holes, mostly on the underside of a leaf. They open to let carbon dioxide in and oxygen out. One of them is called a stoma.
terms.example: The underside of one big leaf can have hundreds of thousands of stomata, each far too small to see.
terms.art: A zoom into the underside of a leaf showing mouth-like openings with two curved guard cells.

terms.meaning: The tiny building block that everything is made of. Atoms are far too small to see. There are only about 90 kinds in nature.
terms.example: A leaf, a cup of water and your fingernail are all made of atoms.
terms.art: A zoom from a leaf to a cluster of tiny coloured balls.

terms.meaning: A few atoms joined together. Atoms join to make molecules, the way letters join to make words.
terms.example: A molecule of water is two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom.
terms.art: A water molecule drawn as a big red ball with two small white balls stuck on, like two ears.

terms.meaning: A kind of atom. It is the main building block of every living thing. The black of charcoal is nearly pure carbon.
terms.example: When a dosa burns black on the tawa, the black is carbon left behind.
terms.art: A burnt black dosa edge next to a lump of charcoal, a little black ball drawn beside them.

terms.meaning: What it takes to make something move, warm up, grow or change. Energy never disappears. It only changes from one kind into another.
terms.example: Sunlight's energy becomes food energy in a mango. When you eat it, it becomes the energy that lets you run.
terms.art: A chain of pictures: the Sun, a mango, a child running.

terms.meaning: A tiny packet of light. Light comes in these packets, far too small to see one at a time.
terms.example: Each second, a leaf in full sunshine is hit by billions of billions of photons.
terms.art: A sunbeam drawn as a stream of tiny glowing dots raining down on a leaf.

terms.meaning: How living things get energy out of their food. They use oxygen to break sugar down, and give out carbon dioxide. Plants do it all day and all night, just like us.
terms.example: A sprouting seed is using their stored food by respiration. They even warm up a tiny bit.
terms.art: A plant and a child side by side, both taking in oxygen and giving out carbon dioxide.

terms.meaning: The tough material that a plant's cell walls are made of. It is made by joining sugars together in a strong, stiff way. Wood, cotton and paper are mostly cellulose.
terms.example: Your cotton shirt was once sugar inside a cotton plant's leaves.
terms.art: A cotton boll, a sheet of paper and a wooden spoon, with a zoom showing straight chains of sugar beads.

terms.meaning: A list of who eats whom, starting from a plant. Energy passes along it, from one living thing to the next.
terms.example: Grass is eaten by a goat, and the goat is eaten by a leopard. The leopard's energy began as sunlight on the grass.
terms.art: Sunlight, grass, a goat and a leopard in a row, joined by arrows.

terms.meaning: Plant-like living things that live in water and make food from sunlight. Some are as big as trees. Most are far too small to see.
terms.example: The green slime on a pond, and seaweed on a beach, are algae.
terms.art: A green pond with slimy algae and a seaweed strand on a beach, with a microscope circle showing tiny green cells.

terms.meaning: Tiny living things, each just one cell, that make food from sunlight. They were the first living things to make oxygen by photosynthesis, billions of years ago.
terms.example: Some of the blue-green scum on a still pond is cyanobacteria.
terms.art: A drop of pond water under a microscope showing blue-green beaded threads.

terms.meaning: Substances in the soil, such as nitrates and iron, that roots take in dissolved in water. Plants need only small amounts. They use them to make things like proteins and chlorophyll.
terms.example: Farmers add manure or fertiliser so the soil has enough minerals.
terms.art: A root hair taking in water with tiny coloured specks dissolved in it.

explanations.definition: Photosynthesis is how green plants make food. Using the energy of light, a leaf joins carbon dioxide and water into sugar. Oxygen is left over and goes out into the air.
explanations.description: A leaf needs two ingredients and a supply of energy. The first ingredient is carbon dioxide, a gas that comes in from the air through tiny holes in the leaf. The second is water, which travels up from the roots. The energy comes from sunlight. It is caught by chlorophyll, the green colouring in the leaf. With that energy, the leaf splits water apart. It joins the hydrogen from the water to carbon dioxide, and builds sugar. The oxygen from the water is left over and goes out into the air. The sugar is the plant's food. Scientists write it in a short way: carbon dioxide plus water, with light, gives sugar plus oxygen.
examples: A tulsi leaf on a sunny windowsill is making sugar right now.
Grass on a cricket ground makes food all day, and makes none at night.
A cactus has no proper leaves. Their green stem does the photosynthesis instead.
explanations.art: A leaf with sunlight shining on it, an arrow of air going in through its underside, water rising up its stalk, a sugar cube inside it and oxygen bubbles leaving.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: how a leaf makes food from light.

explanations.concept: Why leaves are green: chlorophyll catches light
explanations.definition: Chlorophyll is the green colouring in leaves. It soaks up mostly red and blue light, and uses that light's energy to make food. It bounces most of the green light back, so leaves look green to us.
explanations.description: Sunlight looks white, but it is really a mix of all the colours of the rainbow. You can see them when sunlight shines through a glass of water or onto a CD. When light hits something, some colours are soaked up and some bounce off. The colours that bounce off reach your eyes, and that is the colour you see. Chlorophyll soaks up red and blue light very well. It soaks up much less green. So green light bounces back from leaves, and we see green. Leaves also have yellow and orange colourings. They help catch light too, and protect the leaf from too much sun. When a leaf gets old, the green chlorophyll breaks down first. Then the hidden yellow shows through. How a leaf's flat, wide shape helps it catch light is in the unit 'Parts of a plant and their jobs'.
examples: An old leaf on a peepal tree turns yellow before it falls.
A strip of chalk dipped in leaf juice and spirit shows a green band and a yellow band.
Moong sprouts grown in a dark cupboard are pale yellow. Moong makes their green chlorophyll only in light.
explanations.art: A sunbeam split into rainbow colours falling on a leaf. Red and blue arrows go into the leaf, and a green arrow bounces off to a child's eye.
explanations.context: Why are leaves green, and not red or black? This card explains the green colouring that catches sunlight.

explanations.concept: Stomata: how the air gets into a leaf
explanations.definition: Carbon dioxide gets into a leaf through tiny holes called stomata, mostly on the leaf's underside. Oxygen leaves through the same holes.
explanations.description: A leaf looks solid, but its skin has many tiny holes called stomata. Each stoma is a gap between two curved cells shaped like beans, called guard cells. When the plant has plenty of water, the guard cells swell and the stoma opens. Carbon dioxide spreads in, and oxygen spreads out. Water also escapes through the stomata, as invisible water vapour. On a hot, dry day, the plant may close their stomata to save water. Then less carbon dioxide gets in, and the leaf makes less food. So every leaf balances two needs: letting air in, and keeping water. How water climbs up from the roots to replace what escapes is told in the unit 'How water travels through a plant'.
examples: Paint clear nail polish on the underside of a leaf, let it dry, and peel it off with clear tape. Under a toy microscope you can see the shapes of the stomata.
Many desert plants open their stomata only at night, when it is cooler, to save water.
explanations.art: A zoomed-in leaf underside with rows of bean-shaped guard cells around open stomata, carbon dioxide arrows going in and oxygen arrows coming out.
explanations.context: A leaf needs carbon dioxide from the air. This card shows how the air gets inside a leaf.

explanations.concept: From sugar to everything: starch, wood, fruit and you
explanations.definition: Plants turn the sugar they make into everything else they need. They join sugars into starch to store food, and into cellulose to build their walls. They also make oils, proteins and many other things from sugar and minerals.
explanations.description: Sugar is the plant's building material and their fuel. Some sugar is used straight away for energy, the way you use your breakfast. Some is joined into long chains called starch, a store for later. A leaf stores some starch during the day. At night it turns that starch back into sugar and sends it to the rest of the plant. Rice grains, potatoes and wheat are packed with stored starch. Some sugar is joined in a different, stiffer way into cellulose. Cellulose makes wood, cotton, jute and the strings in a banana stem. With minerals from the soil, the plant also turns sugar into oils, like coconut oil, and proteins, like those in dal. So your plate, your clothes and your notebook all began as sugar in a leaf.
examples: A drop of iodine on a potato turns blue-black, because the potato is full of starch.
Your notebook's paper is made of cellulose from trees.
Groundnut oil was once sugar made in a groundnut plant's leaves.
explanations.art: A sugar cube in the middle with arrows out to a grain of rice, a wooden plank, a cotton boll, a bottle of oil and a bowl of dal.
explanations.context: A leaf makes sugar. This card shows how a plant turns that sugar into their whole body, and into most of what we eat and use.

explanations.concept: A tree is built mostly out of air
explanations.definition: Most of the dry weight of a tree comes from carbon dioxide in the air. Water gives a little. The soil gives only a tiny pinch of minerals.
explanations.description: Most people are surprised by this. Take a log of wood and dry out all the water. About half of what is left is carbon. Almost all the rest is oxygen and a little hydrogen. The carbon came from carbon dioxide in the air. Most of the oxygen did too. The hydrogen came from water. Only about one part in a hundred is minerals from the soil. You can see this when wood burns. A whole log on a fire leaves only a small heap of ash. The ash is the soil part. The rest goes back up into the air as carbon dioxide and water vapour, the gases it was built from. Van Helmont's willow showed it too. The tree gained about 75 kilograms in five years, while the soil lost only about 60 grams. He thought the tree was made of water. Water does give the hydrogen. But he did not know that the air has a gas in it that plants build with.
examples: A big log burns down to a handful of ash.
Dried tulsi leaves shrink to a tiny pinch. That pinch came mostly from air.
A sack of rice grew out of carbon dioxide, water and sunlight in a paddy field.
explanations.art: A huge tree drawn as if made of see-through air, with sparkling carbon atoms forming their trunk, and only a tiny pile of soil at their roots.
explanations.context: Where does a tree's wood come from? This card gives the surprising answer, and the evidence for it.

chart.unit: out of every 100 parts by weight

explanations.definition: The oxygen a plant gives out comes from water, not from carbon dioxide. Light's energy is used to split water apart. The plant keeps the hydrogen and lets the oxygen go.
explanations.description: You might guess that a leaf takes carbon dioxide, keeps the carbon and lets the oxygen go. That was a sensible guess, and many scientists believed it. But in the 1930s, a Dutch-American scientist called Cornelis van Niel studied tiny living things that make food from light. They make no oxygen. He suggested that plants split water, not carbon dioxide. In 1941, scientists in California tested this. They gave plants water made with a special, heavier kind of oxygen, which they could follow. The oxygen bubbling out of the plants was the heavy kind. So it came from the water. Splitting water is very hard. A leaf does it with a tiny cluster of manganese and calcium atoms, held in place inside the chloroplast. Chemists still cannot copy it well.
examples: The bubbles rising from a water plant in sunlight are oxygen that was once part of water.
The oxygen you are breathing was split out of water. A plant, or a tiny living thing in the sea, did it.
explanations.art: A water molecule being split by a flash of sunlight, the two small hydrogen balls going into a sugar and the oxygen ball floating away as a bubble.
explanations.context: Leaves give out oxygen. This card answers a tricky question: which ingredient does the oxygen come from?

explanations.concept: Light is energy that comes in packets
explanations.definition: Light carries energy from the Sun. It arrives in tiny packets called photons. Chlorophyll catches photons and uses their energy to make sugar.
explanations.description: The Sun is a giant ball of hot gas. Deep inside it, the smallest atoms, hydrogen, crash together and join into helium. This joining gives off huge amounts of energy. Some of it leaves the Sun as light. The light crosses space and reaches Earth about eight minutes later. When a photon hits a chlorophyll molecule, its energy jumps into it. The leaf passes that energy along, and uses it to split water and build sugar. So the energy in your idli is sunlight, caught by the leaf of a rice plant and stored. When you run, you are using energy that reached a paddy field from the Sun a few months ago. A leaf is not very efficient. A field of crops stores only about 2 out of every 100 parts, often less, of the sunlight that falls on it. The rest bounces away or warms the leaf.
examples: Solar panels on a roof also catch photons, but they turn the energy into electricity instead of sugar.
The energy in a banana you eat today reached the banana plant from the Sun.
explanations.art: The Sun on one side, a stream of glowing dots crossing space, landing on a paddy field, then idlis on a plate, then a child running.
explanations.context: Plants make food using the energy of sunlight. This card follows that energy back to the Sun.

chart.title: Sunlight falling on a field of crops: how much becomes food (an estimate)
chart.unit: out of every 100 parts of sunlight

data.label: Bounced away, or turned into warmth: about 98

explanations.concept: Plants respire too, all day and all night
explanations.definition: Plants use their own sugar for energy by respiration. They take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide, day and night, just as we do. In daylight they make much more oxygen than they use, so overall they give it out.
explanations.description: Plants need energy to grow, to build flowers and to mend themselves. They get that energy by breaking down their own sugar, using oxygen. This is respiration, and every living cell does it, in plants and in people. Roots need oxygen from the air in the soil too. That is one reason plants in soggy, waterlogged soil droop. In the day, photosynthesis is much faster than respiration. So a leaf in sunlight gives out far more oxygen than it uses. At night there is no photosynthesis. The plant only respires, so they take in a little oxygen and gives out a little carbon dioxide. An Indian scientist, Kamala Sohonie, helped show how alike plants and animals are inside. She worked in Cambridge in the late 1930s. She found that cytochrome c, a substance animals use in respiration, is in plants too.
examples: A pile of fresh grass clippings gets warm inside, because the grass cells, and tiny microbes in the pile, are respiring.
A potato in a dark cupboard is respiring slowly. They slowly use up some of their stored food, and go soft.
explanations.art: A plant and a child under a day sky and a night sky. By day the plant breathes out big oxygen bubbles, by night both take in a little oxygen and give out a little carbon dioxide.
explanations.context: People often say plants 'breathe in carbon dioxide'. This card shows the fuller story: plants also use oxygen, all the time.

explanations.concept: Nearly every food chain starts with a leaf
explanations.definition: Plants and algae make their own food from light. Almost every other living being gets their food by eating them, or by eating something that ate them.
explanations.description: Think of your lunch. The rice and dal came from plants. The milk came from a cow that ate grass. The fish ate smaller animals, which ate tiny algae in the sea. Follow any food back far enough and you reach a green thing in the sunlight. Living things that make their own food are called producers. Animals, which must eat, are called consumers. Mushrooms and many bacteria feed on dead plants and animals. They return carbon dioxide and minerals to the air and soil, so plants can use them again. The atoms go round and round. Only the energy comes in fresh each day, as sunlight. The unit on food chains follows this much further.
examples: Grass to goat to leopard.
Tiny algae to small shrimps to a fish to a fisherman's family in Kerala.
A fallen mango rots. Its atoms go back to the air and soil.
explanations.art: A circle: sunlight on a leaf, the leaf eaten by a caterpillar, the caterpillar eaten by a bird, a dead leaf rotting on soil, and atoms drifting back to the plant.
explanations.context: Do animals need photosynthesis? This card shows that almost every meal on Earth began with a leaf in the sun.

explanations.concept: Who made the air we breathe
explanations.definition: There was almost no oxygen in Earth's air for the first two billion years. Tiny living things called cyanobacteria made it, by photosynthesis, very slowly over hundreds of millions of years.
explanations.description: Young Earth's air had nitrogen and carbon dioxide, but hardly any oxygen. Then cyanobacteria appeared in the sea. They were the first to split water with light. Their spare oxygen bubbled out. About 2.4 billion years ago, enough had built up to change the air for ever. Scientists call it the Great Oxidation Event. Later, a bigger cell swallowed a cyanobacterium but did not digest them. The two lived on together. The swallowed one became the chloroplast. The cells that carried it on became algae, and later plants. An American scientist, Lynn Margulis, argued for this idea in 1967. Many scientists thought she was wrong, and her paper was rejected many times. Today the evidence shows she was right. Chloroplasts even have their own small set of genes, like a bacterium.
examples: Every chloroplast in a leaf is descended from a cyanobacterium that once lived on their own.
In some places, like Shark Bay in Australia, cyanobacteria still build rocky mounds called stromatolites, as they did billions of years ago.
explanations.art: A timeline: a reddish young Earth with no oxygen in its air, a blue sea with green threads of cyanobacteria giving off bubbles, then a green land with trees and a child breathing.
explanations.context: This card goes back billions of years. It explains where the oxygen in the air first came from.

explanations.concept: Half of the photosynthesis happens in the sea
explanations.definition: Tiny floating living things in the oceans, called phytoplankton, do about half of all the photosynthesis on Earth. Land plants do the other half.
explanations.description: Phytoplankton are algae and cyanobacteria so small that thousands fit in a drop of seawater. But there are so many of them that together they make about as much food and oxygen as all the forests and fields. One of them, called Prochlorococcus, is probably the most common living thing that does photosynthesis on Earth. Nobody knew they existed until 1988. That year, an American scientist, Penny Chisholm, and her colleagues found them in seawater samples. Scientists can even see phytoplankton from space. Satellites measure the green colour of the sea, which comes from their chlorophyll.
examples: A satellite map of the Bay of Bengal shows greener water where phytoplankton are thick.
About half of the oxygen made on Earth each year is made by tiny living things in the sea.
explanations.art: A drop of seawater magnified to show hundreds of tiny glowing green cells, and a satellite above the ocean picking up the green colour.
explanations.context: People often think forests make all our oxygen. This card shows the hidden half of the story, out at sea.

chart.title: Who makes the oxygen each year (a rough estimate)

data.label: Tiny living things in the sea: about 50

explanations.concept: Is there a quantum trick inside a leaf?
explanations.description: When a photon hits a leaf, its energy must travel through a crowd of chlorophyll molecules. It has to reach a special spot where it is used. It gets there almost without losing any. How? Quantum physics is the science of the very tiniest things. It says that a tiny packet of energy can act like a spreading wave, trying many paths at once. In 2007, scientists in California reported signs of this wave-like spreading inside a light-catching part of a bacterium. It caused great excitement. Some people said plants were using quantum tricks. Since then, scientists have argued about what the signs really mean.
examples: The energy of a photon reaches the right spot in a leaf in less than a billionth of a second.
The wave-like effects were first seen in a bacterium, not in a leaf. This bacterium lives in dim water with no oxygen.

perspectives.who: Graham Fleming, Gregory Engel and colleagues in California, in 2007, and scientists who agreed with them
perspectives.explanation: The energy spreads like a wave through the light-catching parts, and this may help it find the best path quickly.
The wave-like signals are real, but they mostly come from the molecules shaking. They fade too quickly to matter much for how well photosynthesis works.
Quantum physics is certainly at work when chlorophyll catches a photon. Whether nature uses a special quantum trick to move the energy is still argued about.

explanations.art: A crowd of green chlorophyll balls with a glowing energy wave spreading through all of them at once towards a bright centre.
explanations.context: This card follows the energy of light deep inside a leaf, into the strange world of quantum physics, where scientists still disagree.

explanations.concept: Why green? Nobody is quite sure
explanations.description: Here is a puzzle. Sunlight is strongest in the green and yellow part of the rainbow. So why do leaves bounce green light away? A black leaf would soak up everything. Scientists have a few ideas, and none is proved yet.
examples: Some red seaweeds that live deep in the sea do catch green light, using extra colourings.
Solar panels are dark, almost black, because they are built to soak up every colour.

perspectives.who: Shiladitya DasSarma, a scientist in the United States, and others
perspectives.explanation: Perhaps the first living things to use light were purple microbes that soaked up green light. Plants came later and used the colours left over. This is called the Purple Earth idea.
Catching red and blue, and skipping green, may keep the energy coming in at a steady rate. Then a passing cloud or a gust that moves the leaf does not cause sudden jumps the leaf cannot handle.
Too much light can damage a leaf. Bouncing some away may protect it. On a sunny day, leaves often already get more light than they can use.

explanations.art: A green leaf next to an imagined black leaf and a purple microbe, with a big question mark between them.
explanations.context: Leaves are green because chlorophyll bounces green light away. This card asks a harder question: why did plants end up green at all?

explanations.definition: A few living things make food without any light. They use energy from chemicals that seep out of hot cracks in the deep-sea floor. This is called chemosynthesis.
explanations.description: In 1977, scientists dived in a small submarine called Alvin to the dark sea floor near the Galapagos Islands. They found hot springs bubbling out of the rocks. Around them lived giant tube worms, clams and crabs. There was no sunlight at all. The food chain there starts with bacteria that get energy from chemicals in the hot water, instead of from light. So not every food chain starts with a leaf. But on almost all of Earth, light is life's power supply. Even most deep-sea animals still need the oxygen that photosynthesis made.
examples: Giant tube worms near deep-sea hot springs have no mouth. Bacteria living inside them make their food.
Some scientists think life on Earth may have begun near hot springs like these, before photosynthesis existed.
explanations.art: A dark sea floor with a smoking chimney of rock, red-tipped tube worms around it, and a small submarine's lights shining in.
explanations.context: Does all life need sunlight? This card visits a dark place on the sea floor where life found another way.

explanations.description: Scientists around the world are trying to build an artificial leaf. It would use sunlight to split water, or to turn carbon dioxide into fuel. Some early artificial leaves work, but they are expensive, or they break down too fast. Other scientists are trying to make crops better at photosynthesis. Sugarcane and maize use a different, faster way of catching carbon dioxide than rice and wheat do. Since 2008, scientists in a big project have been trying to give rice this sugarcane trick, so rice grows more grain. It is much harder than anyone hoped, and is not finished yet.
examples: A real leaf mends itself every day. No machine can do that yet.
Sugarcane is one of the best plants at turning sunlight into stored sugar.
explanations.art: A shiny artificial leaf made of glass and wire floating in water in sunlight, next to a real green leaf, both with bubbles rising.
explanations.context: Leaves are very good at what they do. This card is about scientists trying to copy them, and to make crops better at it.

explanations.definition: Photosynthesis was not discovered by one person. It was pieced together over more than 300 years, by many people in many countries.
explanations.description: In the first half of the 1600s, Jan Baptist van Helmont showed that a tree is not made of soil. In 1771, Joseph Priestley in England put a sprig of mint in a sealed jar where a candle had burned out. About four weeks later, a candle could burn in that air again. The plant had 'restored' the air. In 1779, Jan Ingenhousz, a Dutch doctor, did hundreds of tests in one summer. He showed that only the green parts of plants do this, and only in light. In 1782, Jean Senebier in Geneva showed that plants need 'fixed air', which we call carbon dioxide. In 1804, Nicolas-Théodore de Saussure showed that water is used too. In the 1940s and 1950s, Melvin Calvin, Andrew Benson and James Bassham in California traced exactly how carbon is built into sugar. In India, Jagadish Chandra Bose wrote a book on photosynthesis in 1924, after years of careful measurements on plants.
examples: Priestley's mint is why people say plants 'freshen the air'.
Ingenhousz showed the same plant did the opposite at night, using up some of the good air.
explanations.art: A row of portraits on a timeline: a man weighing a willow, a mint sprig in a jar with a candle, a doctor watching bubbles on leaves in sunlight, and a lab with glowing flasks.
explanations.context: Who discovered photosynthesis? This card shows that the answer is a long line of people, each adding one piece.

agreed.text: Green plants, algae and cyanobacteria make sugar from carbon dioxide and water, using the energy of light. They give out oxygen.
agreed.evidence: Water plants give off bubbles of oxygen in light and stop in the dark. Leaves kept in the dark make no starch. Scientists have followed the atoms with special labelled kinds of carbon and oxygen since the 1940s.

agreed.text: Most of a plant's dry weight comes from carbon dioxide in the air, not from the soil.
agreed.evidence: Van Helmont's willow gained about 75 kilograms in five years while their soil lost about 60 grams. When wood burns, only a little ash is left. Chemists can measure that dry wood is about half carbon.

chart.title: What dry wood is made from (a rough guide)
chart.unit: out of every 100 parts by weight

agreed.text: The oxygen plants give out comes from splitting water.
agreed.evidence: In 1941, scientists gave plants water made with a heavy kind of oxygen that they could track. The oxygen the plants gave out was the heavy kind.

agreed.text: Plants respire all the time, using oxygen, but in daylight they make more oxygen than they use.
agreed.evidence: Measure the gases around a plant in a sealed box. In light, oxygen goes up. In the dark, it goes down a little and carbon dioxide goes up.

agreed.text: Almost every food chain on Earth begins with photosynthesis, and the oxygen in our air was made by it.
agreed.evidence: Every food can be traced back to a plant or alga. Rocks show that Earth's air had almost no oxygen until cyanobacteria had been making it for a very long time.

agreed.text: Roughly half of the world's photosynthesis happens in the sea.
agreed.evidence: Satellites measure the green chlorophyll in the oceans, and scientists measure how fast phytoplankton grow in seawater samples.

challenging.claim: Plants get their food from the soil, the way we get food from a plate.
challenging.who: An old idea, found in the writings of the ancient Greek thinker Aristotle. Many people still believe it today, including many grown-ups.
challenging.for: Plants sit in soil all their lives and their roots go deep into it. Plants grow better in good soil, and farmers feed the soil with manure.
challenging.against: The soil gives only water and small amounts of minerals, which are like vitamins for the plant. The food itself is made in the leaves, mostly from air. Van Helmont's willow grew by about 75 kilograms while the soil lost only about 60 grams.
challenging.context: This card is about the most common wrong idea about plants: that they eat soil.

challenging.claim: Plants make oxygen, so they never need any.
challenging.who: A common idea, often taught as 'we breathe out carbon dioxide and plants breathe in carbon dioxide'.
challenging.for: Overall, in daylight, plants do give out much more oxygen than they take in.
challenging.against: Every plant cell respires, using oxygen, day and night. Roots in waterlogged soil die because they cannot get oxygen. At night, plants take in a little oxygen.
challenging.context: This card is about a half-true idea: that plants only ever give out oxygen.

challenging.claim: The Amazon rainforest is 'the lungs of the world', and makes 20 out of every 100 parts of our oxygen.
challenging.who: A claim widely shared in news and on social media in 2019
challenging.for: The Amazon is the biggest rainforest on Earth. Its plants do make a huge amount of oxygen.
challenging.against: The forest's animals, fungi and microbes use up almost all of that oxygen again, by breathing and rotting. So the forest adds very little extra. The oxygen in our air built up over millions of years, much of it from the sea. The Amazon still matters hugely, as a store of carbon and a home for millions of kinds of living things.
challenging.context: Rainforests are often called the lungs of the world. This card asks whether that is true.

challenging.claim: Joseph Priestley discovered that plants make oxygen.
challenging.for: In 1771, Priestley showed that a mint plant could 'restore' air in which a candle had burned out. He is also famous for discovering oxygen in 1774, though Carl Scheele in Sweden had found it a little earlier.
challenging.against: Priestley's tests did not always work, and he did not know why. In 1779, Jan Ingenhousz found the reason: plants restore air only in light, and only with their green parts. Ingenhousz explained what Priestley had seen, but he is much less famous.
challenging.context: This card is about who gets the credit for discovering that plants freshen the air.

challenging.claim: The way plants build sugar, the Calvin cycle, was discovered by Melvin Calvin.
challenging.who: Many textbooks, which call it the Calvin cycle
challenging.for: Melvin Calvin led the team in California, and he won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it in 1961.
challenging.against: Andrew Benson and James Bassham did much of the work alongside him. Benson had to leave the lab, and was left out of the prize. Many scientists now call it the Calvin-Benson-Bassham cycle, to share the credit fairly.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous discovery, and the names that were left off it.

challenging.claim: The special sugarcane way of catching carbon dioxide was discovered by Hal Hatch and Roger Slack in Australia, in 1966.
challenging.who: Many biology books, which call it the Hatch-Slack pathway
challenging.for: Hatch and Slack worked out the steps clearly and showed how it worked.
challenging.against: Scientists in Hawaii, led by Hugo Kortschak, had already reported the first clues in sugarcane in 1965. In the Soviet Union, Yuri Karpilov had seen similar results even earlier, in 1960. But he published in Russian, in a journal few outside his country read.
challenging.context: Sugarcane and maize have a clever way of catching carbon dioxide. This card is about who found it first.

challenging.claim: Keeping plants in your bedroom at night is dangerous, because they use up your oxygen.
challenging.who: An idea many families in India and elsewhere have heard
challenging.for: It is true that plants take in a little oxygen at night.
challenging.against: The amount is tiny, far less than one sleeping person or a pet uses. A room with a few pot plants is perfectly safe to sleep in.
challenging.context: This card is about a worry some families have about plants in bedrooms.

challenging.claim: We can fix climate change just by planting enough trees.
challenging.for: Trees are built from carbon dioxide. Growing forests do take carbon out of the air and lock it in wood for a long time.
challenging.against: People now put carbon dioxide into the air far faster than new trees could take it up. Trees also burn or rot one day, and give their carbon back. Most scientists say planting trees helps, but we must also burn much less coal, oil and gas.
challenging.context: Trees take carbon dioxide out of the air. This card asks whether planting trees alone can stop the world from warming.

big_questions.q: If a tree is made mostly of air, why can't you see the tree being built?
big_questions.hint: Can you see the carbon dioxide you breathe out? Things can be real and still invisible.

big_questions.q: The energy in your breakfast came from the Sun. So are you, in a way, running on sunshine?
big_questions.hint: Follow your idli back: rice, leaf, sunlight. Where did the Sun get its energy?

big_questions.q: When a tree burns, where does the tree go?
big_questions.hint: Look at how little ash is left. The rest went back to where it came from.

big_questions.q: You breathe out carbon dioxide, and a tree takes it in. The tree gives out oxygen, and you breathe it in. Where does the air stop and you begin?
big_questions.hint: Some of the carbon in your body was once in a leaf. Some of it may be in a leaf next year.

big_questions.q: A mango is built from air that everyone breathes out, from rain and from sunlight. So who owns it: the person who owns the land, or everyone?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the mango is made of. Which of those things can anyone buy?

big_questions.q: Plants feed almost every animal and made most of the oxygen in the air. Why do people so often notice animals and walk past plants?
big_questions.hint: Think about how slowly plants move, and how quietly they work. Is quiet the same as unimportant?

big_questions.q: A field of crops stores only about 2 out of every 100 parts of the sunlight that falls on it. Is that wasteful, or is it wise?
big_questions.hint: What might happen to a leaf that tried to soak up all the light?

big_questions.q: Tiny sea living things do about half of the photosynthesis on Earth. Nobody had even seen one of the commonest until 1988. What else might be all around us that nobody has noticed yet?
big_questions.hint: Think of things too small, too slow or too ordinary to notice.

big_questions.q: Ingenhousz, Benson and Karpilov did important work but are not famous. Why do some names get remembered and others forgotten?
big_questions.hint: Think about who was in charge, who spoke the most common language and who was in the right place.

big_questions.q: If people one day live on Mars, could plants make their food and air? What would those plants need?
big_questions.hint: Mars has sunlight, a thin air full of carbon dioxide, and ice. What is missing?

big_questions.q: Plants have made food from light for billions of years, and mend their own leaves every day. No machine can yet grow, mend itself and make food from light. What does that tell us about living things?
big_questions.hint: Is something cleverer just because it was made by people?

story.title: A Pinch of Soil
story.note: Kalpatti, Malar, Govindan Mudalali, Saraswathi and the panchayat are made up. The science is real. Nearly 400 years ago, Jan Baptist van Helmont grew a willow in a weighed pot of soil for five years, and the soil hardly changed. In a real pot, the soil can settle a little as it packs together. So a family test may not be quite as tidy as Malar's.
text: In the village of Kalpatti, at the corner where Govindan Mudalali's paddy field met the dusty lane, there stood a mango tree so wide that a whole wedding party could sit in their shade. Nobody alive remembered planting the tree. But everybody remembered their mangoes.

Every summer, the children of the lane waited under their branches with their mouths already watering. Ripe mangoes thudded onto the lane, and into the field, and onto the tin roof of the little house where Malar lived with her mother. Her mother swept under the tree every morning. 'A tree that feeds everybody deserves a clean floor,' she said.

That summer, Govindan Mudalali, the richest man in the village, built a wall. He built it of new red bricks, right round the tree, with an iron gate and a padlock. He hung a board on the gate. It said PRIVATE.
'The tree stands in my field,' he told anyone who asked. 'Their roots go deep into my soil. Every mango is made of my land. So every mango is mine.'

The children stopped waiting under the tree. The mangoes fell inside the wall and were loaded into the Mudalali's cart for the market. Malar's mother stopped sweeping. She did not say anything about it, which was worse.
Malar was nine, and she did not like the word PRIVATE. She liked the word made even less. Made of my land. It sat in her head like a stone in a shoe.

At school, Revathi Miss had once drawn a leaf on the blackboard with arrows going in and out. 'Leaves make food,' she had said, 'from sunlight, water and air.' Everybody had copied it into their notebooks. Nobody had believed it, least of all Malar. Air was nothing. You could not build a mango out of nothing.

That evening, Malar watered the tulsi in the clay pot by their door. Her mother had planted this tulsi the year Malar was born, from a seed no bigger than a mustard seed. Now the tulsi was a bush as tall as Malar's waist. Every winter her mother cut them back and gave bunches of their leaves to the whole lane, and every spring they grew again.
On the inside of the pot, just above the soil, there was a scratch. Her mother had made it with a nail on the first day, so she would know when the soil sank and needed more.
Malar looked at the scratch. She looked at the bush. She looked at the scratch again.
The soil was still on the line.
Nine years of leaves. Nine winters of tulsi for the whole lane. And the soil had not gone down. Malar sat back on her heels with her mouth open. The tulsi had not been eating the soil at all.

The panchayat met on Thursday under the neem tree by the well. The sarpanch, Saraswathi, was a small woman with spectacles and a fat ledger. When Malar stood up and asked to speak, some of the men laughed. Govindan Mudalali laughed loudest.
'Speak, kanna,' said Saraswathi.

Malar set the tulsi pot down on the mat. It was heavy, and she was out of breath from carrying it. 'Mudalali says the mangoes are made of his soil,' she said. 'This tulsi is nine years old. If they were made of soil, the soil would have gone down. But look. It is still on Amma's line.'
People leaned forward. Somebody held up a lantern. The soil sat exactly on the scratch.
'Then what are they made of?' said Saraswathi.

'Partly water,' said Malar. 'But when Amma dries tulsi leaves for tea, the water goes, and a big heap shrinks to a tiny pinch. The pinch is still there. Revathi Miss says leaves make food out of air, in the sunlight. I didn't believe her. But it can't be the soil. So it must be the air.'
'Air!' Govindan Mudalali threw up his hands. 'Air is nothing! You cannot build a tree out of nothing.'

Malar had thought about this all night. 'When your cook burns a big log in the kitchen fire, Mudalali, where does it go? There is only a handful of ash in the morning. The rest goes up in the smoke, into the air. It goes back where it came from.' She took a breath. 'The ash is the soil part. Only a handful.'
Nobody laughed now. Old Muthu, who had burned wood in his kiln for fifty years, slowly nodded.
Saraswathi wrote for a long time in her ledger. Then she looked over her spectacles at the Mudalali. 'Govindan. Did you buy the air above your field?'
'Who buys air?'
'And the sunlight that falls on the tree?'
'Nobody can buy sunlight.'
'And the rain?'
'The rain falls on everyone,' said the Mudalali, a little more quietly.

'Then the panchayat finds,' said Saraswathi, 'that the mango tree is made of air, which all of us breathe out, and of sunlight and rain, which belong to nobody. And of a pinch of soil.' She closed the ledger. 'The pinch is yours, Govindan. You may keep a pinch of the mangoes.'
The laughter that rolled round the well was so loud that the crows flew out of the neem tree. Even the Mudalali's own servants laughed. The Mudalali went the colour of a ripe mango himself.
The wall stayed. But on Saturday morning the padlock was gone, and the iron gate stood open. Malar's mother took her broom and went out to sweep.

That afternoon, Malar lay on her back under the mango tree, in the speckled shade. She breathed out slowly, all the way, until her chest was empty. Somewhere above her, a leaf in the sunlight was taking that breath and keeping it.
Next summer, she thought, a little bit of me will be a mango.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the tree is not made of soil. Malar's clue is the scratch in the tulsi pot. Years of growth, and the soil has not gone down. A plant's dry body is built mostly from carbon dioxide in the air. It is joined with water using the energy of sunlight. Only a tiny pinch is minerals from the soil. Burning shows it too: a log goes back into the air and leaves a little ash, the soil part. The story also quietly asks who owns what is made from things everyone shares.
ask: Govindan Mudalali said every mango was made of his land. What clue showed Malar that this was wrong?
Why did Malar's mother scratch a line inside the tulsi pot?
When a big log burns, only a little ash is left. Where did the rest go?
Saraswathi said the Mudalali could keep a pinch of the mangoes. Why a pinch?
Malar breathed out under the tree. Why did she think a bit of her would become a mango?

printables.title: A plant mat for each player
items: A pot with an empty plant outline: spaces for roots, stem, leaves, flowers and seeds
A small 'Leaf Kitchen' box where you trade ingredients for sugar

rules: Each player starts with a plant mat, 1 LEAF tile and 2 of each ingredient card.
On your turn, first take one weather and life card and do what it says.
Then take 1 SUNLIGHT, 1 WATER and 1 CARBON DIOXIDE card from the piles.
Leaf Kitchen: for each LEAF you have, you may trade 1 SUNLIGHT, 1 WATER and 1 CARBON DIOXIDE for 1 SUGAR. Each time, put 1 OXYGEN bubble into the middle of the table, for the air.
Spend SUGAR to build tiles on your plant mat. More leaves let you make more sugar.
The first plant to build at least 1 root, 1 stem, 3 leaves, 1 flower and 1 seed wins. Then count the oxygen bubbles together. That is the air your plants made for everyone.

flow.do: 1. Give each player a plant mat, 1 LEAF tile and 2 of each ingredient card. 2. Put the ingredient piles, the sugar tokens and the oxygen bubbles in the middle. 3. Shuffle the weather and life cards face down.
flow.say: In this game, each of us is a plant. We cannot eat. We must make our own food in our leaves, from sunlight, water and carbon dioxide.
flow.kid: You are a plant! You cannot eat food. You make it in your leaves. You need sunlight, water and carbon dioxide.
flow.context: This is the first step of Leaf Kitchen. It is a card game where each player is a plant that makes their own food by photosynthesis. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: Play one practice trade together. Hand in 1 SUNLIGHT, 1 WATER and 1 CARBON DIOXIDE. Take 1 SUGAR. Put 1 OXYGEN bubble in the middle.
flow.say: Let's make our first sugar. Sunlight, water and carbon dioxide go in. Sugar comes out for the plant. And look, a bubble of oxygen goes out into the air.
flow.kid: Make your first sugar. Hand in sunlight, water and carbon dioxide. Take a sugar. Put an oxygen bubble in the middle.

check.q: In the Leaf Kitchen, what comes out besides the sugar?
check.why: When a leaf makes sugar, oxygen is left over. It goes out into the air, and we breathe it. Picking 'carbon dioxide' usually means thinking plants give out the same gas we breathe out. Leaves take carbon dioxide in, and give oxygen out. Picking 'soil' usually means thinking the plant's food comes from the soil.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. Draw a weather and life card, then collect 3 ingredient cards. 2. Trade ingredients for sugar in the Leaf Kitchen. 3. Build tiles. 4. Read the QUESTION cards aloud and answer them together.
flow.say: Watch what happens on a NIGHT card. You can't make sugar, but you still have to pay sugar. Plants respire all the time: they use up food for energy, day and night.
flow.kid: Take turns. Draw a card and do what it says. Make sugar. Build your plant. On a NIGHT card, you still pay sugar. Plants use food all night!

ask.q: Why is building more leaves a good plan?
good: Each leaf is a kitchen, so two leaves can cook twice as much.

ask.q: What did the DRY SPELL card do, and why?
good: The leaf closed its stomata to save water.
So no carbon dioxide could get in, and it couldn't make sugar.

flow.parent: Good answers to the question cards. Oxygen goes out into the air, for animals and people to breathe. The soil gives water and a few minerals, not food. Leaves are green because chlorophyll bounces green light back. If a child runs out of sugar, let them carry on. Real plants also struggle on long cloudy spells.

flow.do: When someone wins, stop. Count the oxygen bubbles in the middle together.
flow.say: Look how many oxygen bubbles our plants made. Who gets to breathe that air?
flow.kid: Count the oxygen bubbles in the middle. Your plants made all that air! Who breathes it?
flow.think: Your plant made oxygen for everybody. Where does the oxygen in your room come from right now?

flow.do: Ask one last question about the game.
flow.say: Where did your plant's whole body come from in this game? Did any of it come from the soil?
flow.kid: Look at your finished plant. What was your plant built from? Was any of that soil?

check.q: In the game, your plant was built from sugar. Where did the sugar come from?
check.why: Every tile was paid for with sugar, and every sugar was made in a leaf from sunlight, water and carbon dioxide. Real plants work the same way. Picking 'the soil' is the most common idea, even among grown-ups. The soil gives only water and a pinch of minerals.

games.context: This is a card game about how a plant makes their food. Each player is a plant. You trade sunlight, water and carbon dioxide for sugar in your leaves, and spend the sugar to grow.

games.title: Photon Relay
games.players: 3 or more players, in a big room, a terrace or outdoors

printables.title: Role cards to hang round your neck
Light batons and atom balls
items: 10 black 'carbon' balls (crumpled black paper or socks)

printables.title: Energy chain sheet
items: How many hands did the energy pass through?
Where did the carbon balls end up?

rules: The SUN stands at one end. The LEAVES stand in the middle, next to a basket of black carbon balls, which is the 'air'.
The SUN runs light batons to a LEAF, one baton on each trip. Only a leaf can take light.
When a LEAF holds 3 light batons, it picks up one carbon ball. The ball with its 3 batons is now one sugar.
The CATERPILLAR may take a sugar from a leaf. The BIRD may take it from the caterpillar. The MONGOOSE may take it from the bird.
At each handover, the giver drops one baton into a 'warmth' bucket and passes on the ball and the batons that are left. This is the energy used up for living.
Anyone holding a carbon ball with no batons left has no energy left. They sit down. The FUNGUS takes their carbon ball and throws it back into the air basket.
The CLOUD may stand between the SUN and a LEAF and block it for 10 seconds.

flow.do: 1. Give out the role cards. 2. Put the SUN at one end of the room. 3. Put the air basket of black carbon balls by the LEAVES.
flow.say: This game shows how the Sun's energy travels into a leaf, and then from animal to animal. The black balls are carbon atoms from the air.
flow.kid: Pick a role card. The Sun gives out light. Only leaves can catch it. The black balls are carbon from the air.
flow.context: This is the first step of Photon Relay, a running game. A photon is a tiny packet of light. The game shows how sunlight's energy passes from a leaf into animals.

flow.do: 1. The SUN runs light batons to the LEAVES. 2. A leaf with 3 batons picks up a carbon ball, which becomes a sugar. 3. Animals take the sugar along the chain. 4. At each handover, the giver drops one baton in the warmth bucket.
flow.say: Only the leaves can catch light. Everybody else has to get their energy by eating. Watch the warmth bucket fill up.
flow.kid: Run the light to a leaf. Leaves turn carbon into sugar. Animals pass the sugar along. Drop a baton in the warmth bucket each time.

ask.q: Why can't the bird take light straight from the Sun?
good: Only leaves have chlorophyll to catch light.
Animals must eat to get energy.

ask.q: What happens to the light batons in the warmth bucket?
good: That energy is lost as warmth.
Each animal uses some energy to live, so less goes on.

flow.parent: The real rule behind the bucket is this. At each step of a food chain, most energy is used up for living and lost as warmth. In the game, the mongoose gets a carbon ball with no batons left. Real top hunters get only a tiny share of the Sun's energy. That is why there are many more blades of grass than tigers.

flow.do: Play one round with the CLOUD blocking the Sun, and with the FUNGUS returning carbon balls to the air.
flow.say: What happens to the whole chain when the cloud blocks the light? And what does the fungus do with the carbon?
flow.kid: Now the cloud blocks the Sun. What happens to everyone? Watch the fungus. Where do the carbon balls go?

check.q: In the game, what did the fungus do with the carbon balls?
options: Put them back into the air, so leaves could use them again
check.why: Fungi and bacteria rot dead things. They give the carbon back to the air as carbon dioxide, so plants can build with it again. Carbon goes round and round. Energy does not. It comes in fresh each day as sunlight. Picking 'thrown away for ever' usually means thinking dead things simply vanish.

flow.do: Sit down together and fill in the energy chain sheet.
flow.say: So which comes in fresh every day, and which goes round and round: the light, or the carbon?
flow.kid: Fill in the sheet. Which goes round and round? Which comes new each day from the Sun?
flow.think: The carbon in your body has been in leaves, animals and air many times before. Who might it have belonged to?

games.context: This is a running game based on the founder's 'photon relay' idea. Players pass light from the Sun to leaves, and sugar from leaves to animals. It shows that energy comes from the Sun and carbon goes round and round.
