items.p: During photosynthesis, some things go into a leaf, some are made and kept, and one goes out into the air. Sort them.
cats: Made and kept in the plant
items: Made and kept in the plant
Made and kept in the plant
items.a: see items
items.why: Light, water and carbon dioxide go in. The plant makes sugar, and stores some of it as starch. Oxygen is left over and goes out. A strong answer does not put oxygen and carbon dioxide the wrong way round.

items.p: The green colouring in leaves that catches sunlight is called ____.
items.why: Chlorophyll catches the energy in sunlight. The leaf uses that energy to make food.

items.p: Arjun says, 'Plants take in oxygen to make their food, just like we do.' What has he mixed up?
opts: To make food, a leaf takes in carbon dioxide and gives out oxygen
Plants do not make food at all
items.why: Photosynthesis takes in carbon dioxide and gives out oxygen. Arjun is half right about one thing: plants also use a little oxygen all the time to get energy from their sugar, as we do. A strong answer separates making food from using it.

items.p: Meenakshi puts sunk spinach discs in baking-soda water, and leaves the cup in a dark cupboard for 25 minutes. What will she see?
opts: The discs stay at the bottom
items.why: In the dark, the leaf cannot make food, so it makes no oxygen. With no bubbles, the discs stay sunk. Picking 'all float up' means thinking carbon dioxide alone is enough. The leaf needs light as well.
items.context: In the Rising Leaf Discs, you sink small circles of spinach leaf in water. When a leaf makes oxygen, tiny bubbles make the circles float up.

items.p: Plants grow big because they suck food up out of the soil.
items.why: False. A plant makes their own food, sugar, in their leaves, from carbon dioxide and water, using light. The roots take up water and a pinch of minerals. A strong answer says where the food is really made.

items.p: Each of these foods is a part of a plant, full of food that the leaves made. Match each food to the part it is.
pairs: a swollen stem under the ground
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Leaves make sugar. The plant sends it to other parts and stores it, often as starch. That is why seeds, stems and roots can be full of food.

items.p: In the starch picture experiment, the black paper is clipped on both sides of the leaf, top and bottom. Why?
opts: So no light at all reaches that part of the leaf
So the leaf does not fall off
To stop the iodine getting in
items.why: The test asks: does a leaf make starch only where light falls? So the covered part must get no light at all, from above or below. A strong answer says what the test is checking.
items.context: In the starch picture experiment, you clip a black paper shape on a leaf for two sunny days. Then you test the leaf for starch with iodine, which turns blue-black on starch.

items.p: Your aunt adds fertiliser to her potted plant and says, 'This is the plant's food.' Is she right? Explain.
items.a: A strong answer says not quite. Fertiliser gives minerals, which a plant needs in small amounts, a bit like vitamins. The plant's real food is sugar, which the leaves make from carbon dioxide and water, using sunlight.
items.why: Many people call fertiliser 'plant food'. The answer should say what fertiliser does and where the real food is made.

items.p: Carbon dioxide gets into a leaf through tiny holes, mostly on the underside. These holes are called ____.
items.why: Stomata open to let carbon dioxide in and oxygen out. They close when the plant is short of water.

items.p: Lakshmi moves a lamp from 40 cm away to 10 cm away from a water plant. What happens to the bubbles?
opts: More bubbles come, because the light is brighter
Fewer bubbles come, because the plant gets too hot
items.why: Brighter light gives the plant more energy, so they make food and oxygen faster. Picking 'too hot' is a careful thought, which is why the lamp should be an LED that stays cool. A strong answer links light to how fast oxygen is made.
items.context: In the bubble count, a water plant sits in a glass of water. They give off bubbles of oxygen as they make food. A lamp is put close by, far away, or switched off.

items.p: After the Rising Leaf Discs, write three sentences. What did you guess before? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
items.a: For example: I guessed the discs in the dark would float too. I saw all 10 discs float in the sunny baking-soda cup, and none in the other two. I think the leaf needs light and carbon dioxide to make oxygen, and the oxygen bubbles lifted the discs.
items.why: A strong answer is honest about the guess, gives what was seen with a number, and gives a reason using light and carbon dioxide.
items.context: In the Rising Leaf Discs, you sink small circles of spinach leaf in water. When a leaf makes oxygen, tiny bubbles make the circles float up.

items.p: Draw a leaf. Draw arrows for what goes in and what comes out. Then draw where the sugar goes.
items.a: Arrows in for sunlight, water and carbon dioxide. An arrow out for oxygen. An arrow from the leaf down the stem to the roots, fruit or a growing tip, labelled sugar.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the sugar staying inside the plant, because the plant uses it to live and grow.
items.art: An empty leaf outline with space around it for arrows.

items.p: Kavya's family in Chennai argue about keeping potted plants in the bedroom at night.

views.says: Take the plants out at night. They breathe out carbon dioxide in the dark and steal our oxygen.
Keep lots of plants. Plants give us oxygen, so they make the bedroom healthier.
One plant is enough. Plants make the room calm and pretty, but water left in their saucers breeds mosquitoes.

items.ask: How many plants would you keep in the bedroom? Use what you learned about what plants do in the light and in the dark. Then say one fair point from someone you disagree with.
items.a: Any choice can be strong. A strong answer uses the science, for example: in the dark a plant only respires, but a few pots use far less oxygen than one sleeping person, so Paati's worry is very small. In the day they give out oxygen, but too little to change a room much, so Kavya's reason is small too. Then it is fair to another side, for example: Amma is right that mosquitoes are a real problem.
items.why: Paati is right that plants give out carbon dioxide at night. Kavya is right that they give out oxygen in the day. The amounts in a bedroom are small either way, so other things, like mosquitoes or how the plants make you feel, can decide it. There is no single right answer.

items.p: A leaf can make food only while light falls on it.
items.why: True. Light gives the energy to join carbon dioxide and water into sugar. In the dark, the leaf stops making food, though the plant keeps using the food already made.

items.p: Name three foods you ate today. For each one, say how it began with a leaf in the sunlight.
items.a: For example: my dosa was made from rice and urad dal, the seeds of plants whose leaves made sugar in the sun. My curd came from a cow who ate grass. My banana grew on a banana plant whose leaves made the sugar in it.
items.why: A strong answer traces each food back to a plant, even animal foods, because animals eat plants.

items.p: Put these steps of photosynthesis in order.
items: The leaf uses that energy to join carbon dioxide and water
Sugar is made, and oxygen goes out into the air
The plant uses the sugar to live and grow
items.a: order shown
items.why: Light comes first, because it gives the energy. Sugar and oxygen come out of the joining. A strong answer puts the sugar to use at the end.

items.p: Look at the chart from the bubble count. About how many bubbles would you expect in one minute with the lamp 30 cm away?
items.why: 30 cm is between 20 cm, which gave 16 bubbles, and 40 cm, which gave 6. So the answer should be between 6 and 16. Picking 'about 40' would mean the plant made more oxygen in dimmer light. A strong answer uses the pattern to predict.
items.context: In the bubble count, a water plant sits in a glass of water. They give off bubbles of oxygen as they make food. A lamp is put close by, far away, or switched off.

chart.title: Made-up example: bubbles from a water plant in one minute
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what results can look like. Your numbers will be different.

items.p: In Burn It Back to Air, the dry twigs weighed 50 grams. After burning, the ash weighed about 1 gram. Where did the other 49 grams go?
opts: Into the air, as carbon dioxide and water vapour
Into the light of the fire
items.why: Burning turns the wood back into the gases it was built from. The ash is the small part that came from the soil. Picking 'nothing' means thinking things can vanish. A strong answer says the wood went back where it came from: the air.
items.context: In Burn It Back to Air, a grown-up burns a few dry twigs outdoors in a steel bowl. You weigh the twigs before, and the ash after.

items.p: When you blew into limewater through a straw, it turned ____. This showed that your breath has carbon dioxide in it.
items.why: Carbon dioxide reacts with the lime and makes tiny bits of chalk, which make the water milky. The same gas is what trees are built from.
items.context: In The Breath a Tree Eats, you make limewater from chuna, the lime paste in paan, and blow into it through a straw.

items.p: Most people guess that a tree is built from soil. Give two pieces of evidence from this unit that it is not.
items.a: Any two. For example: Van Helmont's willow gained about 75 kilograms while the soil lost only about 60 grams. Burning twigs leaves only a tiny heap of ash. In the story, the soil in the tulsi pot stayed on the scratched line for nine years. In my own pot, the plants got heavier but the soil did not get lighter.
items.why: A strong answer gives real evidence, with numbers where it can, and says what each one shows.

items.p: Scientists once thought the oxygen a leaf gives out comes from carbon dioxide. In 1941, a test with a special kind of oxygen showed where it really comes from. Where?
opts: From water, split by light's energy
items.why: The leaf uses light's energy to split water. It keeps the hydrogen to build sugar, and lets the oxygen go. Scientists had believed it came from carbon dioxide, which was a sensible guess. A test settled it.

items.p: A plant uses oxygen only at night.
items.why: False. A plant respires all the time, day and night, using oxygen to get energy from sugar. In daylight they make much more oxygen than they use, so we only notice the using at night.

items.p: Sort these living beings. Who makes their own food from light, and who must eat?
items.a: see items
items.why: Plants, seaweed and cyanobacteria photosynthesise. A mushroom is not a plant. They feed on dead leaves and wood. A strong answer puts the mushroom with the eaters, even though they grow in the ground.

items.p: Put this food chain from the sea near Kochi in order, starting with where the energy comes from: sardine, Sun, a person eating fish curry, tiny floating algae, tiny shrimp.
items.a: order shown
items.why: In the sea, tiny algae do the photosynthesis. Shrimp eat the algae, sardines eat the shrimp, and people eat the sardines. Every step started with sunlight caught by the algae.

items.p: In the Hidden Colours activity, yellow and orange bands climbed the chalk with the green. Old peepal leaves turn yellow before they fall. Why?
opts: The green chlorophyll breaks down, and the yellow that was always there shows
The leaves fill up with yellow water
Yellow is the colour of tired leaves
items.why: The chalk showed that green leaves already hold yellow colours. The green covers them until the chlorophyll breaks down. A strong answer uses the chalk result as evidence.
items.context: In the Hidden Colours activity, you crush leaves in spirit and stand a stick of chalk in the green liquid. The colours climb the chalk in bands.

items.p: In Build a Sugar, you took apart 6 carbon dioxides and 6 waters and built one sugar. You had 12 red oxygen balls left over. What are they in a real leaf?
opts: The oxygen the leaf gives out into the air
items.why: The 12 leftover oxygen atoms pair up into 6 oxygen molecules, which go out of the leaf. Nothing was lost and nothing new was made. A strong answer says atoms are only rearranged.
items.context: In Build a Sugar, you build molecules from clay balls: black for carbon, red for oxygen and white for hydrogen.

items.p: Where does the oxygen we breathe come from? Three people answer differently.

views.says: From forests like the Amazon. That is why people call them the lungs of the Earth.

views.who: Dr Shalini, who studies the sea
views.says: About half of all photosynthesis happens in the sea, in tiny floating algae and cyanobacteria too small to see.

views.who: Selvi, a forest officer in the Nilgiris
views.says: A big forest makes lots of oxygen, but the animals, fungi and rotting wood in it use almost all of it again. Forests matter most because they store carbon and bring rain.

items.ask: Whose answer do you think is most useful? Give a reason. Then say what one of the others gets right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one and gives evidence, for example: Dr Shalini, because half of photosynthesis is in the sea, which most people forget. Then it is fair to another, for example: Kavya is right that forests make a lot of oxygen, and Selvi is right that they also use it.
items.why: This is a real argument. In 2019 many news stories called the Amazon the lungs of the world. Scientists pointed out that a mature forest uses up almost all the oxygen it makes. Each view has some truth.

items.p: In the story, Malar's mother scratched a line inside the tulsi pot, just above the soil. If the tulsi really ate soil, what would the line show after nine years?
items.a: A strong answer says the soil would have sunk far below the line, because nine years of leaves and stems would have used it up. But the soil was still on the line. So the tulsi was not built from soil.
items.why: This asks the child to say what the evidence would look like if the wrong idea were true. That is how a test tells two ideas apart.
items.context: In this unit's story, A Pinch of Soil, Malar lives in the village of Kalpatti with her mother and a nine-year-old tulsi plant.

items.p: A cactus has no proper leaves, only spines. Where does a cactus make their food? Why might this help in a desert?
items.a: A strong answer says a cactus makes food in their thick green stem, which has chlorophyll. Without wide leaves, less water escapes. Many cacti open their stomata only at night, when it is cooler.
items.why: Any green part of a plant can photosynthesise. The answer should name the green stem and link it to saving water.

items.p: Draw yourself and a tree. Draw the gases that pass between you, with arrows and labels. Add the sunlight.
items.a: An arrow from me to the tree labelled carbon dioxide. An arrow from the tree to me labelled oxygen. Sunlight shining on the tree's leaves.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the loop: we breathe out what plants build with, and plants give out what we breathe in.

items.p: Match each part of a plant to its job in photosynthesis.
pairs: takes in water and a few minerals
let carbon dioxide in and oxygen out
carries water up and sugar around the plant
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Photosynthesis happens in the leaves, but the whole plant helps. A strong answer gives each part a different job.

items.p: Van Helmont decided that his willow tree was made of water. What did he not know about?
opts: The carbon dioxide in the air, which plants build with
items.why: He saw that the soil hardly changed, and he gave only water, so water seemed the only answer. Nobody yet knew that air has a gas in it that plants build into sugar. Water does give the hydrogen. A strong answer says he was partly right.
items.context: Nearly 400 years ago, Jan Baptist van Helmont grew a willow in a weighed pot of soil for five years, giving it only rainwater.

worksheets.title: Light, Atoms and the History of Air (challenge)

items.p: Sunlight gives a leaf the energy to make sugar. But light is not made of atoms. So is a tree 'made of sunlight'? Explain your thinking.
items.a: A strong answer says no, not the material. A tree's body is built of atoms, mostly carbon and oxygen from carbon dioxide, and hydrogen from water. Sunlight gives the energy that joins them. Some of that energy is stored in the wood, which is why wood burns and gives out heat and light.
items.why: This separates the building blocks, atoms from air and water, from the energy, which comes from the Sun.

items.p: Deep inside the Sun, hydrogen atoms join to make helium and give off energy. How is this linked to the idli you ate for breakfast?
opts: The energy reached Earth as light, a rice plant stored it in starch, and you got it from the idli
The idli was cooked by the Sun
The idli is made of helium
items.why: Sunlight carries the Sun's energy. Rice leaves caught it and stored it in the grain as starch. Eating the idli gives you that energy. A strong answer follows the energy step by step.

items.p: Earth's air has had plenty of oxygen ever since Earth formed.
items.why: False. For about the first two billion years there was almost no oxygen. Tiny cyanobacteria in the sea made it by photosynthesis, very slowly. A strong answer says oxygen in the air was made by living beings.

items.p: Lynn Margulis argued in 1967 that chloroplasts, the tiny green parts in leaf cells, were once something else. Many scientists thought she was wrong. Now most agree with her. What were chloroplasts once?
opts: Free-living cyanobacteria, taken inside a bigger cell long ago
items.why: Chloroplasts have their own small set of genes and split in two like bacteria. That evidence convinced other scientists. A strong answer notes that an idea many people rejected turned out to be right.

items.p: Is planting trees enough to stop the world getting warmer? Three people disagree.

views.who: Thulasi, aged 10, who plants saplings in Coimbatore
views.says: Plant millions of trees. Trees are built from carbon dioxide, so they pull it out of the air.
We put carbon dioxide into the air far faster than trees can take it out. We must burn much less coal and petrol.
Trees help, but they need land and water. If every field becomes forest, where will our food grow?

items.ask: What do you think should be done? Use what you know about what trees are built from. Then answer back from one other person's side.
items.a: A strong answer uses the science, for example: trees do lock carbon from the air into wood, so planting helps. It also weighs another side, for example: Farzana is right that trees are too slow on their own, and trees give their carbon back when they burn or rot.
items.why: Most scientists say planting trees helps, but it is not enough by itself. Land and water are real limits too. There is no single right answer.

items.p: In 1771, Joseph Priestley put a mint plant in a closed jar where a candle had burned out. Some days later, a candle could burn in the jar again. Why?
opts: The plant had given out oxygen, which a flame needs
The plant had made the jar warmer
The plant had eaten the smoke
items.why: A flame uses up oxygen. In light, the mint plant made oxygen by photosynthesis, so the air could keep a flame going again. Priestley did not yet know the name of the gas. A strong answer names oxygen and the light the plant needed.

items.p: Scientists still argue about why leaves are green and not black. One idea is that black leaves would soak up too much light and get damaged. How could you test whether too much light harms a leaf?
items.a: For example: take two of the same potted plant. Keep one in normal sunlight and put the other under much stronger light for the same number of hours. Give both the same water. After a week, compare the leaves for pale or brown patches.
items.why: A strong test changes only the amount of light, keeps everything else the same, and says what to look for. It is fine to say the answer is not known yet.

items.p: A field of crops stores only about 2 out of every 100 parts of the sunlight that falls on it. What happens to most of the rest?
opts: It bounces away, or warms the leaves and the ground
It is stored in the soil
It goes back to the Sun
items.why: Most sunlight is reflected, or soaks in and becomes warmth. Leaves often get more light than they can use. Picking 'turned into oxygen' mixes up energy with atoms. The oxygen comes from water.

items.p: In the story, Saraswathi told the Mudalali he could keep 'a pinch of the mangoes'. Explain the science behind her joke.
items.a: A strong answer says a mango tree is built mostly from carbon dioxide in the air and water from rain, using sunlight. Only a tiny pinch, the minerals, comes from the soil. So if the Mudalali owns only the soil, he owns only a pinch of the tree.
items.why: The answer should say what the tree is made of, and link the tiny soil part to the pinch.
items.context: In this unit's story, Govindan Mudalali says every mango on a big old tree is his, because the tree grows in his field. Saraswathi is the head of the village panchayat.

items.p: Imagine every plant and alga on Earth stopped photosynthesis tomorrow. What would run out first, food or oxygen? Explain.
items.a: A strong answer says food would run out first. Every food chain starts with plants and algae, and animals would soon have nothing to eat. The air holds a huge store of oxygen, so it would last much longer, but slowly be used up by breathing and rotting.
items.why: This asks the child to compare two effects and reason about which is faster.

items.p: Astronauts are planning a greenhouse on Mars, lit by lamps. Why would they choose red and blue lamps, not green ones?
opts: Chlorophyll soaks up red and blue light best, and bounces much of the green away
Red and blue lamps are warmer
items.why: Leaves use mostly red and blue light. Much green light bounces off, so green lamps would feed the plants less well for the same electricity. A strong answer links the lamp colour to what chlorophyll does.
items.context: In Lunch on Mars, you design a greenhouse where plants make food and air for astronauts.

items.p: Plants join many sugars together into a long chain to store food for later. This store is called ____.
items.why: Rice, potatoes and wheat are full of starch. Iodine turns blue-black on it.

items.p: Draw the journey of one carbon atom: from your breath, into a leaf, into a mango, into you, and back into the air.
items.a: A loop of at least four pictures with arrows: a child breathing out, a leaf taking in carbon dioxide, a mango growing, the child eating the mango, and an arrow back to the breath.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the atom going round. Carbon is used again and again. Only the energy comes in fresh, from the Sun.
items.art: An empty circle of four boxes joined by arrows.

items.p: Match each test in this unit to what it showed.
pairs: a leaf needs light and carbon dioxide to make oxygen
a leaf makes starch only where light falls
most of the wood goes back into the air
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each test gives one piece of evidence. Together they show how a leaf builds food from air and water, using light.

items.p: Every food chain on Earth begins with sunlight.
items.why: False, though nearly all do. Near hot springs on the deep sea floor, bacteria make food using energy from chemicals in the water, with no light at all. Worms, crabs and fish live on them. A strong answer says 'nearly all' and names the exception.

items.p: Dry wood is about half carbon. Most of the rest is oxygen, with a little hydrogen. Scientists say a tree is built mostly from air, not mostly from water. Why?
opts: Most of the dry wood's weight is carbon and oxygen that came from carbon dioxide
Water is too heavy to build with
Air is too light to build anything
items.why: Dry wood is about half carbon, and most of the rest is oxygen, and both came from carbon dioxide in the air. Water gives the hydrogen, which is light. Picking 'trees drink very little water' is not right. Trees take up huge amounts of water, but most of it goes out of the leaves again.

experiments.title: The Rising Leaf Discs
experiments.question: Does a leaf need light and carbon dioxide to make oxygen?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which discs will float up first: the ones in the light, the ones in the dark, or the ones in plain water? Will some not float at all? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Keep everything the same except one thing. Use discs from the same leaves, the same number of discs, the same cups and the same amount of liquid. Cup A and cup B both have baking soda water. Only the light changes. Cup A and cup C are both in the light. Only the baking soda changes.
results_table: Cup A: light, baking soda (discs floating)
Cup B: dark, baking soda (discs floating)
Cup C: light, plain water (discs floating)

materials.item: fresh spinach (palak) leaves
a plastic syringe, 10 or 20 ml, from a chemist shop. Ask for one without a needle, or ask the chemist to keep the needle.
baking soda, a quarter of a teaspoon
one drop of washing-up liquid
a drinking straw or a hole punch, to cut discs
3 clear glasses or cups, labelled A, B and C, and a glass of water that was boiled and has cooled
a sunny window or balcony, or a bright LED desk lamp, and a cardboard box to make cup B dark
a clock or timer, a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: Use a syringe with no needle. Do not drink the baking soda water. A grown-up helps with the syringe, as the first few tries are tricky.

schedule.what: Cut leaf discs, sink them, and count how many float in each cup every 3 minutes, for up to 25 minutes.

experiments.record: Fill in the table every 3 minutes. Then draw a bar for each cup, as tall as the number of discs floating at the end.

flow.do: 1. Stir a quarter teaspoon of baking soda into one glass of water, about 300 ml. Add one drop of washing-up liquid. 2. Take the glass of boiled and cooled water. Add one drop of washing-up liquid. 3. Label three cups A, B and C.
flow.say: Baking soda puts carbon dioxide into the water, in a form that leaves can use to make food. Boiling drives the carbon dioxide out of water, so the boiled water has very little. That is the only difference.
flow.kid: Stir baking soda into one glass of water. The other glass has boiled water, now cool. Add one drop of soap to each. Label three cups A, B and C.
flow.parent: The soap helps the liquid soak into the leaf. Baking soda water holds carbon dioxide that the leaf can use. Tap water often holds some carbon dioxide, which is why cup C uses water that was boiled and left to cool.
flow.context: This is the first step of the leaf disc experiment. Tiny circles of spinach leaf are sunk in water. If they make oxygen, the bubbles make them float back up.

flow.do: 1. Press the end of a straw onto a spinach leaf, between the big veins. Twist to cut out a disc. 2. Cut 30 discs. 3. Keep them in two piles of 20 and 10.
flow.say: Cut between the big veins. The veins are like stiff pipes and they get in the way.
flow.kid: Press the straw onto the leaf and twist. Out pops a little green circle. Cut 30 circles. Avoid the thick veins.

flow.do: 1. Take the plunger out of the syringe. Drop in 10 discs. 2. Push the plunger back in, nearly to the discs. 3. Suck up 5 ml of baking soda water. 4. Put a finger tightly over the tip. Pull the plunger back hard and hold for 10 seconds. 5. Let go and tap. Repeat until the discs sink. 6. Do this twice more: once more with baking soda water, then, after rinsing the syringe, with the boiled water.
flow.say: Pulling the plunger sucks the air out of the leaf. The liquid rushes in, and the discs get heavy and sink. Now they're empty of air, ready to start.
flow.kid: Put 10 circles in the syringe. Suck up a little baking soda water. Finger over the tip. Pull back hard. Let go. Repeat until they sink.
flow.parent: It can take 3 or 4 pulls before the discs sink. If some still float, leave them out. You need 10 sunk discs for each cup.

flow.do: 1. Tip the discs sunk in baking soda water into cups A and B, with baking soda water. 2. Tip the boiled-water discs into cup C, with boiled water. 3. Put A and C in bright sun, or 10 cm under a bright lamp. 4. Put B under a box in the same place.
flow.say: A and C get light. B is in the dark. Now we count. Every 3 minutes, we write down how many discs are floating in each cup.
flow.kid: Cups A and C go in the bright light. Cup B goes under a box. Every 3 minutes, count the floating circles.

flow.do: 1. Every 3 minutes, count the floating discs in each cup and write the numbers in the table. 2. Lift the box off cup B quickly to look, then put it back. 3. Stop when all the discs in cup A float, or after 25 minutes.
flow.say: Look closely at the discs in cup A. Can you see tiny bubbles on them? Where do you think the bubbles came from?
flow.kid: Count every 3 minutes. Write it in the table. Look closely at cup A. Can you see tiny bubbles? What could they be?

ask.q: Why do you think the discs float up?
good: The leaf makes a gas, and the bubbles lift it.
Gas inside the disc makes it lighter than water.

chart.title: Made-up example: discs floating in the sunny cup, minute by minute
chart.note: Nothing happens for a few minutes. Then the discs rise one by one, as oxygen gathers inside them.

flow.parent: The bubbles are oxygen, made by the leaf from water as it makes food. Let your child guess before you say so. In strong sun, the discs in cup A usually float within 10 to 20 minutes. Under a lamp it can take 20 to 30 minutes, so keep counting a little longer if you need to. If a few discs in cup C rise late, the water still held a little carbon dioxide. If nothing floats in cup A after 25 minutes, the light was too weak or the leaves were old. Try again with fresh leaves in direct sun.

flow.do: Compare the three cups at the end. Help your child draw one bar for each cup.
flow.say: Which cup floated? Which cups stayed sunk? What was different about them?
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each cup. Which cup's circles floated? What did that cup have that the others didn't?

check.q: Only the discs in cup A floated: light and baking soda water. What does that show?
options: Leaves need light and carbon dioxide to make oxygen
check.why: Cup B had carbon dioxide but no light, and stayed sunk. Cup C had light but almost no carbon dioxide, and stayed sunk. Only cup A had both, so only cup A made oxygen. Picking 'baking soda makes anything float' is a fair worry. But cup B had baking soda too, and its discs did not float. That is why we had three cups.

chart.title: Made-up example: leaf discs floating at the end, out of 10
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what results can look like. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a leaf needs light and carbon dioxide to make oxygen. What I saw: after 15 minutes, all 10 discs floated in the sunny baking soda cup, cup A. None floated in the other two cups. Why: the leaf used light to make food from carbon dioxide and water. The spare oxygen made the discs float.

experiments.context: In this experiment you sink tiny circles of spinach leaf in water. In light, a leaf makes oxygen, and the bubbles make the circles float. You test what the leaf needs: light, carbon dioxide, or both.

experiments.title: The Starch Picture: a leaf that keeps a secret
experiments.question: Does a leaf make starch only where light falls on it?
experiments.predict: Guess first. You will cover part of a leaf with a black paper shape for two sunny days. Then you will test the leaf for starch. Which part will turn blue-black: the covered part, the uncovered part, or all of it? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use one leaf, so the plant, the water and the warmth are the same for both parts. Only the light changes. The covered part gets no light. The rest of the same leaf gets light.

materials.item: a potted plant with thin, soft leaves that stands in direct sun for at least 3 hours a day, such as balsam, geranium, or a bean plant grown from a rajma seed for two or three weeks. Thick, waxy leaves like money plant work badly.
black paper or kitchen foil, and two paper clips
povidone-iodine solution, the brown antiseptic sold by chemists
surgical spirit or rubbing alcohol, half a small steel tumbler. A liquid hand sanitiser that is mostly alcohol also works, more slowly. Both catch fire easily.
a small steel tumbler, a big bowl, and very hot water from a kettle or a pan
a white plate, a spoon, and a slice of raw potato and some cooked rice for practice

experiments.safety: Surgical spirit catches fire very easily. Never heat it on a stove or near a flame. Warm it only by standing its tumbler in hot water from a kettle, with the stove switched off. Only a grown-up handles the hot water and the spirit. Iodine stains and must not be swallowed.

schedule.what: Practise the iodine test on potato and rice. In the evening, clip a black paper shape on both sides of one leaf. Put the plant in the sunniest place.
Check the plant has had sun and water. Leave the shape on.
In the afternoon, pick the leaf. A grown-up softens it and takes out its green colour. Test it with iodine and see the picture.

experiments.record: Draw the leaf with its shape before the test. Then draw it after the iodine, colouring the blue-black parts. Fill in the table.

flow.do: 1. Put a slice of raw potato and a spoon of cooked rice on a white plate. Add a pinch of sugar and a pinch of salt. 2. Mix 10 drops of iodine with about 50 drops of water in a small cup. 3. Put one drop on each food.
flow.say: Iodine is brown. But when it touches starch, it turns blue-black. Starch is the food store plants make from sugar. Which of these foods have starch?
flow.kid: Put a drop of brown iodine on each food. Watch the colour. Blue-black means starch is there. Which foods have starch?

good: Not the sugar or the salt.

flow.context: This is the first step of the starch picture experiment. First you learn the iodine test: brown iodine turns blue-black where there is starch.
flow.parent: Starch turns dark blue or almost black within a few seconds. Sugar and salt stay brown.

flow.do: 1. In the evening, cut a simple shape from black paper, like a star or your child's first letter. Cut a matching plain square. 2. Clip the shape on top of one big leaf and the square underneath, so no light gets through. 3. Put the plant where they get the most direct sun. Water them as usual.
flow.say: Under the shape, the leaf will be in the dark for two whole days. All around it, the leaf gets sunshine. Our question is, where will it make starch?
flow.kid: Cut a black paper star or your first letter. Clip it on a big leaf. Put the plant in the sun for two days.
flow.wait: Leave the plant in the sun for 2 days.
flow.parent: You do not need to keep the plant in a cupboard first. Each night a leaf sends its starch away, so the covered part uses up its old starch over the two days. If the days are cloudy, leave the shape on for one more sunny day.

flow.do: 1. In the afternoon, pick the leaf and take off the paper. 2. A grown-up dips the leaf in just-boiled water for 1 minute, to soften it. 3. Put the leaf in a small steel tumbler with spirit. 4. Stand the tumbler in a bowl of very hot water, with the stove off. 5. Wait 10 to 15 minutes, until the leaf is pale. If the water cools first, pour in fresh hot water.
flow.say: The green colour would hide the iodine colour. So we wash the green out with spirit. The spirit catches fire easily, so it never goes near the stove.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up for this part. They soften the leaf in hot water. Then they wash out its green colour. Watch the spirit turn green!
flow.parent: Never heat spirit directly or near a flame. Very hot water is enough, and the spirit may bubble gently. The leaf goes pale and a little stiff. Rinse it in warm water so it softens again.

flow.do: 1. Rinse the pale leaf in warm water and spread it flat on the white plate. 2. Cover it with the diluted iodine. 3. Wait 2 minutes, then rinse gently and look.
flow.say: A picture has appeared. Where is it blue-black, and where is it pale?
flow.kid: Spread the pale leaf on the plate. Cover it with iodine. Wait 2 minutes. What picture appears?

check.q: After the iodine test, the leaf is blue-black everywhere except the star shape. What does that show?
options: The leaf made starch only where light fell on it
Iodine does not work on leaves
The leaf makes starch best in the dark
check.why: Blue-black means starch. The covered star got no light, so that part made no food and stayed pale. The rest of the leaf got light, made sugar, and stored it as starch. Picking 'best in the dark' usually means mixing up starch with something that was kept safe under the paper. The paper only blocked the light.

flow.parent: Starch shows as dark blue, dark purple or almost black. Leaf with no starch stays yellow-brown. If the whole leaf stays brown, the plant did not get enough sun, or this plant stores little starch in their leaves. Try again in a sunnier spot, or with a leaf from another plant. If the star is only a little paler than the rest, leave the shape on for one more sunny day next time.

flow.do: Lay the tested leaf next to your drawing from before. Compare them.
flow.say: In the 1860s, a German scientist called Julius Sachs did tests like this. He showed that leaves make starch only in the light.
flow.kid: Put your leaf next to your first drawing. Does the pale shape match the paper star? A scientist did this test over 160 years ago!
flow.think: Could you write a secret message on a leaf, using only light?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a leaf makes food only where light falls on it. What I saw: after iodine, the leaf turned blue-black everywhere except the star shape, which stayed pale. Why: blue-black means starch, and starch is stored food. The leaf needs light to make it, and under the star there was no light.

experiments.context: In this 3-day experiment, you cover part of a leaf with a black paper shape. Then you test the leaf for starch, the food it stores. The test shows a picture of where light fell.

experiments.title: Count the Bubbles: a water plant and a lamp
experiments.question: Does a water plant make more oxygen in brighter light?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the plant give off more bubbles when the lamp is close, far away, or switched off? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same piece of water plant, in the same glass of water, all the time. Change only how far away the lamp is. Count for exactly one minute each time. Count each distance twice, because one count can be a fluke.
results_table: Average (add the two counts and halve)

materials.item: a sprig of hydrilla or another water plant, about 10 cm long, from an aquarium shop. If you cannot get one, use the leaf disc kit instead: put a cup of sunk discs at 10, 20 and 40 cm from the lamp, and count how many float after 15 minutes.
a tall clear glass of water, with a pinch of baking soda stirred in
a paper clip, to weigh the plant down
a bright desk lamp with an LED bulb, and a ruler
a clock or timer that counts seconds

experiments.safety: Keep the lamp and its wire away from the water. Use an LED bulb, which stays cool. A grown-up places the lamp.

schedule.what: Count bubbles from a water plant with the lamp at 10, 20 and 40 cm, and with the lamp off.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar for each lamp distance, as tall as the average number of bubbles.

flow.do: 1. Stir a pinch of baking soda into a tall glass of water. 2. A grown-up cuts the end of the water plant cleanly. 3. Slide a paper clip onto the sprig and drop it in, cut end up.
flow.say: Pond plants make their food under water. The baking soda gives them extra carbon dioxide. Watch the cut end.
flow.kid: Stir a pinch of baking soda into the water. Clip the plant so they sink. Put the cut end at the top.
flow.context: This is the first step of the bubble count. A water plant gives off bubbles of oxygen as they make food. You count the bubbles with a lamp close by and far away.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up puts the lamp 10 cm from the glass, measured with a ruler. 2. Wait 3 minutes for the plant to get going. 3. Count the bubbles from the cut end for exactly one minute. 4. Count again for another minute.
flow.say: We wait first, because the plant needs time to get used to the new light. Then we count for exactly one minute.
flow.kid: Lamp 10 cm away. Wait 3 minutes. Then count the bubbles for one minute. Count again for another minute.

flow.do: 1. Move the lamp to 20 cm. Wait 3 minutes and count twice. 2. Move it to 40 cm. Wait and count twice. 3. Switch the lamp off and close the curtains. Wait and count twice.
flow.say: Each time, only the distance changes. Same plant, same glass, same minute. That keeps the test fair.
flow.kid: Now move the lamp to 20 cm. Count twice. Then 40 cm. Count twice. Then switch it off. Count again.

ask.q: What happened to the bubbles when the lamp moved further away?

flow.parent: Bubbles usually come in a stream from the cut end. If they come too fast to count, count for 30 seconds and double it. If there are almost no bubbles at 10 cm, the lamp is too weak. Put the glass in direct sun for 10 minutes, then compare sun, shade and a dark cupboard instead. A fresh sprig and a little more baking soda also help. A few bubbles may still come in the dark at first, from gas already inside the plant.

flow.do: Find the average for each distance: add the two counts and halve. Help your child draw a bar chart.
flow.say: Let's draw one bar for each lamp position. Which bar is tallest?
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each lamp place. Make each bar as tall as its number. Which is tallest?

check.q: With the lamp 10 cm away, the plant made 30 bubbles a minute. At 40 cm, they made 6. With the lamp off, they made none. What does this show?
options: More light makes the plant make oxygen faster
The lamp's heat makes the bubbles
The plant makes bubbles best in the dark
check.why: The closer the lamp, the brighter the light on the plant, and the faster they made oxygen. With no light, they made none. Picking 'the lamp's heat' is a good scientist's worry. That is why we used a cool LED bulb. It hardly warmed the water, but it still changed the bubbles.

flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a water plant makes oxygen faster in brighter light. What I saw: with the lamp 10 cm away, they gave 30 bubbles a minute. At 40 cm they gave only 6, and with the lamp off, none. Why: the plant uses light's energy to make food and split water, so more light means more oxygen.

activities.title: Where Did the Giant Come From?

materials.item: a seed of a big tree, such as a mango stone, a tamarind seed or a neem fruit
a big tree to look at: from a window, on the street, or in a photo
a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: If you go out to a tree, go with a grown-up. Do not climb the tree.

schedule.what: Hold a big tree's seed, look at the tree, and write down your guess about where the tree came from.

activities.record: Write your guess: the tree came mostly from soil, water, air or sunlight? Keep the page. You will look at it again at the end of the unit.

flow.do: 1. Put a mango stone, or another big tree's seed, in your child's hand. 2. Look together at a big tree, from a window, on the street, or in a photo. 3. If a tree is close by, try to hug their trunk.
flow.say: A big tree started as a seed like this one. Look at the trunk and the branches. What do you notice? What do you wonder?
flow.kid: Hold the seed. Now look at a big tree. A seed like this grew into this tree! What do you notice? What do you wonder?

ask.q: What do you wonder about this tree?
good: How did they get so big?

flow.context: This is the first step of Where Did the Giant Come From? You visit a big tree and hold one of their seeds. It is the noticing activity that starts the unit.

flow.do: Ask where all the tree's wood came from. Give four choices: soil, water, air or sunlight. Let your child choose and give a reason. Do not tell them the answer.
flow.say: The seed was tiny. Now the tree weighs more than a lorry. Where did all that wood come from? The soil, the water, the air, or the sunlight?
flow.kid: The seed was tiny. The tree is huge. Where did all the wood come from? Soil, water, air or sunlight? Choose one.
flow.parent: Most children, and most grown-ups, say the soil. That is a fine guess. Don't correct it now. The unit lets your child find out, which is much more powerful than being told.

check.q: Your guess: where did most of this tree's wood come from?
check.why: This is a guess, so any answer is fine for now. Most people say the soil, because roots sit in it. The surprising answer is the air. Leaves take in carbon dioxide and build it into wood, using sunlight's energy and a little water. You will see the evidence in this unit.

flow.do: Write your child's guess and reason on a page, with the date. Keep it.
flow.say: Let's write your guess down, with your reason. At the end, we'll see if you still think the same.
flow.kid: Write down your guess and why. Keep the page safe. You will check it at the end.
flow.think: If the tree really were made of soil, what would you see around their roots?

activities.context: This is the opening activity of the unit. You hold a big tree's seed, look at a tree, and guess where all the tree's wood came from.

activities.title: The Breath a Tree Eats

materials.item: chuna, the edible lime paste sold at paan shops, one teaspoon
two clean glasses, water and a drinking straw

activities.safety: Chuna stings eyes and skin. A grown-up mixes it. Never suck through the straw, only blow gently. Do not drink the limewater. Wash hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Make limewater the night before. Blow into it and watch it turn milky.

activities.record: Draw the glass before and after blowing. Write one sentence: my breath has carbon dioxide in it.

flow.do: 1. The night before, stir one teaspoon of chuna into a glass of water. 2. Leave it to settle overnight. 3. In the morning, gently pour the clear top part into a clean glass. That clear liquid is limewater.
flow.say: Limewater is a detector. It turns milky when carbon dioxide gets into it.
flow.kid: A grown-up makes limewater from chuna. It looks clear like water. But it is a secret detector for carbon dioxide!
flow.context: This is the first step of The Breath a Tree Eats. You make limewater from chuna, the lime paste used in paan. Limewater turns milky when carbon dioxide gets in.

flow.do: Your child blows gently through a straw into the limewater, for about a minute, with small slow breaths.
flow.say: Blow out slowly through the straw. Never suck. Watch the water.
flow.kid: Blow gently into the limewater through the straw. Never suck! Keep blowing slowly. Watch what happens.

check.q: The limewater turned milky when you breathed into it. What does that show?
options: Your breath has carbon dioxide in it
Your breath has milk in it
check.why: Limewater turns milky when carbon dioxide gets into it. The cloudiness is tiny bits of chalk, made when carbon dioxide meets the lime. So your breath carries carbon dioxide out of your body. Picking 'your breath is dirty' is a natural thought. But carbon dioxide is not dirt. It is a clean gas, and leaves build food from it.

flow.do: Talk about where the carbon dioxide in your breath goes next.
flow.say: A grown-up breathes out about a kilogram of carbon dioxide every day. A child breathes out about half that. Some of it drifts to a leaf. The leaf takes it in and builds it into sugar, and then into wood or fruit.
flow.kid: Every breath sends out carbon dioxide. A leaf can take it in. It can turn it into sugar, wood or a mango!
flow.parent: Your breath's carbon dioxide came from your food. Your body used that food for energy, by respiration, with the help of oxygen. So the carbon in your breath was once in a plant, and may soon be in a plant again.

flow.do: Sit facing a pot plant or a tree. Breathe out slowly towards them. Then breathe in slowly.
flow.say: Breathe out to the plant. They can take in your carbon dioxide. Breathe in. Some of the oxygen you take in was made by leaves. Let's do it five times, slowly.
flow.kid: Sit by a plant. Breathe out slowly to them. Then breathe in slowly. You and the plant are sharing air. Do it five times.
flow.think: The carbon dioxide you breathe out can become part of a leaf. Where does the air stop and the plant begin?

activities.context: In this activity, you make limewater from chuna, the lime paste in paan. You breathe into it and it turns milky. This shows your breath carries carbon dioxide, the gas a tree is built from.

activities.title: The Hidden Colours of a Leaf

materials.item: a few spinach or coriander leaves
a stick of white chalk
a little surgical spirit, rubbing alcohol or liquid hand sanitiser that is mostly alcohol, in a small steel bowl
a spoon, and an old CD or a glass of water for making a rainbow

activities.safety: Surgical spirit catches fire easily. Keep it far from the stove, candles and diyas. A grown-up handles it. Work by an open window.

schedule.what: Make a rainbow with a CD. Then separate the colours in a leaf with chalk and spirit.

activities.record: Draw the chalk and colour in the bands you see. Label which band you think is chlorophyll.

flow.do: 1. Hold an old CD in sunlight, shiny side up, and tilt it until a rainbow shows on a wall. 2. Or stand a glass of water on a sunny windowsill and look for a rainbow on the floor.
flow.say: Sunlight looks white. But it is really all the colours mixed. Leaves use mostly the red and the blue. They bounce the green back to our eyes.
flow.kid: Tilt the CD in the sunlight. See the rainbow? Sunlight has all these colours. Leaves use the red and blue. Green bounces back.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Hidden Colours of a Leaf. First you see that sunlight is a mix of colours.

flow.do: 1. Tear the leaves into small pieces into the steel bowl. 2. Add spirit until it just covers them. 3. A grown-up crushes them hard with the back of a spoon until the spirit is dark green.
flow.say: We're squeezing the colours out of the leaf. The spirit washes them out.
flow.kid: Tear the leaves into tiny bits. A grown-up adds spirit and crushes them. Watch the liquid turn green.

flow.do: 1. Stand the chalk upright in the bowl, so its bottom 1 cm is in the green liquid. 2. Wait 10 to 15 minutes. 3. Watch the colours climb the chalk.
flow.say: The liquid creeps up the chalk. Different colours travel at different speeds, so they come apart into bands.
flow.kid: Stand the chalk in the green liquid. Wait and watch. The colours climb up. Do they all go the same height?

ask.q: What colours can you see on the chalk?
good: A yellow or orange band higher up.

check.q: The chalk showed a green band and a yellow band. Why do old leaves turn yellow before they fall?
options: The green chlorophyll breaks down, and the yellow that was always there shows through
The leaf is painted yellow by the sun
Yellow is made only in autumn
check.why: The chalk shows that a green leaf already has yellow colours hidden in it. The green chlorophyll covers them up. When a leaf gets old, the plant breaks down their chlorophyll first, to save the useful parts. Then the yellow shows. Picking 'painted by the sun' usually means thinking the colour comes from outside the leaf.

flow.do: Let the chalk dry. Look at the bands together.
flow.say: The green band is chlorophyll, the colour that catches light. The yellow helps catch light too, and protects the leaf from too much sun.
flow.kid: The green band is chlorophyll. It catches the light. The yellow helps too. Every green leaf has hidden yellow inside!
flow.think: Why do you think leaves are not black, which would soak up every colour?

activities.context: In this activity, you make a rainbow to see the colours in sunlight. Then you separate the colours inside a leaf, using chalk and spirit. You find out what makes leaves green.

activities.title: Build a Sugar from Air and Water

materials.item: 36 small balls of clay or atta dough: 6 black (or brown), 18 red and 12 white. Coloured beads or paper balls also work.
toothpicks or matchsticks with the heads cut off
two plates, one labelled IN and one labelled OUT

activities.safety: If you use toothpicks, take care with the sharp points. Do not eat raw dough.

schedule.what: Build 6 carbon dioxides and 6 waters from balls. Take them apart and rebuild them into one sugar and 6 oxygens.

activities.record: Draw your sugar molecule. Write how many black, red and white balls it has.

flow.do: 1. Explain the colours: black is carbon, red is oxygen, white is hydrogen. 2. Build 6 carbon dioxide molecules: one black ball with a red ball on each side. 3. Build 6 water molecules: one red ball with two white balls. 4. Put them all on the IN plate.
flow.say: These are models of the molecules a leaf takes in. Carbon dioxide from the air, and water from the roots. Real ones are far too small to see.
flow.kid: Black is carbon. Red is oxygen. White is hydrogen. Make 6 carbon dioxides: red, black, red. Make 6 waters: white, red, white.
flow.context: This is the first step of Build a Sugar, based on the founder's building-block game. You build models of carbon dioxide and water, then rebuild them into sugar, the way a leaf does.

flow.do: 1. Take all the molecules apart. Sunlight's energy is what does this in a real leaf. 2. Build one sugar: a ring of 5 black balls and 1 red ball, with the sixth black ball sticking out. Add the rest of the red and white balls round it, 12 white and 6 red altogether. 3. Put it on the OUT plate.
flow.say: In a real leaf, sunlight's energy breaks the molecules apart. Then the atoms join up again in a new way. Nothing is lost. Nothing new is made. They are only rearranged.
flow.kid: Pull them all apart. That is sunlight's job in a leaf. Now build one sugar. It needs 6 black, 12 white and 6 red.
flow.parent: The real sugar, glucose, has 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen and 6 oxygen atoms. Its shape is a ring of 5 carbons and 1 oxygen, with the sixth carbon on a little arm. A neat model does not matter. The counting is what matters.

flow.do: Count the balls left over. Join them into pairs, and put them on the OUT plate.
flow.say: We have 12 red balls left over. Join them in pairs. Each pair is one oxygen molecule, the oxygen we breathe. That is what the leaf lets go.
flow.kid: Count the red balls left over. Join them in pairs. These are oxygen! The leaf lets them float away.

check.q: You built a sugar and had 12 red balls left over. What are they in a real leaf?
options: Oxygen, which floats out into the air
check.why: The leftover red balls are oxygen atoms. They pair up to make oxygen molecules, which float out of the leaf for us to breathe. Picking 'they disappear' usually means thinking things can vanish. In real life, atoms are never lost. They are only rearranged.

flow.do: Look at the IN plate and the OUT plate together.
flow.say: Every single ball on the OUT plate was on the IN plate. A tree is built this way, one sugar at a time, from air and water.
flow.kid: Count all the balls on the OUT plate. Are they the same as at the start? A tree is built like this!
flow.think: The atoms in a sugar were once in the air. Where might they go after you eat the sugar?

activities.context: In this activity, you build models of molecules from clay balls. You take apart carbon dioxide and water and rebuild them into sugar and oxygen, the way a leaf does in sunlight.

activities.title: Burn It Back to Air

materials.item: a handful of very dry twigs, about 20 grams
a kitchen scale, a steel plate or an old steel bowl, and matches
a bucket of water

activities.safety: Only a grown-up lights and tends the fire. Do it outdoors or on an open terrace, on a bare stone or cement floor, away from cloth, dry grass and wind. Keep a bucket of water beside you. Children watch from at least one big step away.

schedule.what: Weigh some dry twigs. A grown-up burns them outdoors. Weigh the ash.

activities.record: Write the weight of the twigs and the weight of the ash. Draw the heap of twigs and the heap of ash side by side.

flow.do: 1. Weigh the dry twigs on the kitchen scale in a steel bowl. 2. Write down the weight.
flow.say: These twigs were built by a tree, from air, water and a pinch of soil. Let's weigh them before we burn them.
flow.kid: Weigh the dry twigs in the bowl. Write down the number. Guess how much ash will be left.
flow.context: This is the first step of Burn It Back to Air. A grown-up burns some dry twigs, and you compare their weight with the ash left over.

flow.do: 1. Outdoors, a grown-up puts the bowl on the ground and lights the twigs. 2. Let them burn down completely. 3. Let the bowl cool for a few minutes.
flow.say: Watch the twigs. Where do you think the wood is going?
flow.kid: Stand back one big step. A grown-up lights the twigs. Watch. Where is the wood going?
flow.parent: If black, half-burned bits are left, that is charcoal, which is carbon not yet burned. Stir it so it burns to grey ash.

flow.do: 1. When the bowl is cold, weigh the ash. 2. Compare it with the weight of the twigs.
flow.say: How much was left? Twenty grams of twigs usually leave less than one gram of grey ash. Where did the rest go?
flow.kid: Weigh the cold ash. Compare it with the twigs. Where did all the rest go?

check.q: 20 grams of twigs burned down to less than 1 gram of ash. Where did most of the wood go?
options: Into the air, as carbon dioxide and water vapour
check.why: Burning joins the wood's carbon and hydrogen with oxygen again. They leave as carbon dioxide and water vapour, the same gases the tree built the wood from. The little ash is the minerals that came from the soil. Picking 'nothing' usually means thinking things can vanish. Atoms never vanish. They only move and rearrange.

flow.parent: A kitchen scale may show 0 or 1 gram for the ash, because it is so light. Both mean almost nothing was left. The rest went into the air as carbon dioxide and water vapour.

activities.context: In this activity, a grown-up burns a few dry twigs outdoors. You weigh them before and after. Most of the wood goes back into the air, showing that it came from the air.

activities.title: Sunbeam Dance

materials.item: some open space, and a yellow and a green towel or cloth

activities.safety: Clear the space of anything you could bump into.

schedule.what: Dance the story of photosynthesis, from night to sunrise.

activities.record: Draw your favourite moment of the dance.

flow.do: 1. One dancer is a SUNBEAM, with the yellow cloth. 2. The others are LEAVES, with the green cloth, curled up on the floor. 3. The room is dim. It is night.
flow.say: It's night. The leaves are resting and only breathing gently. They can't make any food without light.
flow.kid: Curl up small. You are a leaf at night. Breathe slowly. You can't cook food in the dark.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Sunbeam Dance, from the founder's dance ideas. One dancer is sunlight. The others are leaves, waking up to make food.

flow.do: 1. Open the curtains, or switch on the lights. 2. The SUNBEAM dances in and touches each leaf. 3. Each leaf slowly opens up. It breathes in air with big arms, and 'cooks' with a stirring movement. 4. It breathes out oxygen with a long whoosh.
flow.say: Sunrise! The sunbeam touches each leaf. Open up. Breathe in the air. Stir your sugar. Now breathe out oxygen for everyone.
flow.kid: Sunrise! When the sunbeam touches you, open up. Scoop in air. Stir your sugar. Whoosh out oxygen!
flow.think: In the dance, the sunbeam had to touch every leaf. In the real world, what happens to leaves in the shade?

flow.do: End with everyone standing tall as one tree, arms up like branches. Take three slow breaths together.
flow.say: Now we are one tall tree, built from all that sugar. Breathe slowly, three times.
flow.kid: Stand tall like a tree. Arms up like branches. Breathe slowly three times. A tree is built from sugar made with light.

activities.context: This is a short dance. One dancer is a sunbeam and the others are leaves. The leaves wake up in the light, take in air, make sugar and breathe out oxygen.

setup.caption: 1. Leaves curl up. It is night.

setup.caption: 2. The sunbeam dances in. Each leaf wakes up and makes food.

setup.art: Children standing together with arms raised like branches of one big tree.
setup.caption: 3. Finish as one tall tree. Breathe together.

projects.title: Van Helmont's Willow, in Five Weeks

materials.item: a medium plastic or clay pot with a hole, and a saucer
potting soil from a plant nursery, or garden soil, enough to fill the pot
6 rajma, chana or maize seeds, weighed dry and then soaked overnight
a kitchen scale that weighs in grams
a sheet of newspaper, a notebook and a pencil

projects.safety: Wash hands after handling soil. Ask a grown-up to help lift the pot onto the scale.

schedule.what: Spread the soil on newspaper in the sun to dry. Weigh the 6 dry seeds, then soak them overnight.
Weigh the dry soil and the pot. Plant the seeds you weighed dry and soaked overnight.
Check the seedlings. Measure the tallest. Water only with clean water.
Measure and draw the plants. Stop watering for the last few days so the soil starts drying.
Gently take out the plants. Shake and brush the soil off the roots back into the pot. Weigh the plants. Spread the soil to dry again.
Weigh the dried plants and the dried soil. Compare everything. Write what you found.

projects.record: Fill in this table: dry seed weight, plant weight fresh, plant weight dried, soil weight at the start, soil weight at the end. Then write one sentence about where the plants came from.

flow.do: 1. Spread the soil thinly on newspaper in the sun for a day, to dry it. 2. Weigh the 6 dry seeds together and write it down. 3. Soak the seeds in water overnight.
flow.say: Wet soil is heavier than dry soil. So we dry it first. Then we weigh the soil, not the water in it. We weigh the seeds dry for the same reason.
flow.kid: Spread the soil on newspaper in the sun. Weigh the dry seeds. Then soak them. Wet things weigh more!
flow.context: This is the first step of Van Helmont's Willow, in Five Weeks. You copy a famous experiment from nearly 400 years ago, weighing soil before and after plants grow in it.
flow.wait: Leave the soil to dry in the sun for 1 day.

flow.do: 1. Weigh the empty pot. 2. Fill it with the dry soil and weigh it again. 3. Write both numbers in the notebook. 4. Plant the soaked seeds and water them. 5. Put the pot in the sunniest place you have.
flow.say: Van Helmont did exactly this, nearly 400 years ago. He weighed his soil and his little tree. Then he waited five years. We'll wait five weeks.
flow.kid: Weigh the empty pot. Weigh it full of dry soil. Write each number down. Plant the seeds in a sunny place.
flow.parent: To find the weight of the soil alone, take the empty pot's weight away from the full pot's weight. Keep the saucer and any spilled soil, so nothing is lost.

flow.do: 1. Once a week, measure the tallest plant with a ruler and draw the pot. 2. Water only with clean tap water or rainwater. 3. Do not add any manure or fertiliser. 4. Stop watering for the last three days, so the soil starts drying.
flow.say: We are giving the plants only water. Watch what they build.
flow.kid: Each week, measure the tallest plant. Draw them. Give only clean water. No plant food!
flow.wait: Check once a week for about 4 weeks.

flow.do: 1. When the plants are about four weeks old, gently pull them out. 2. Shake and brush every bit of soil off the roots back into the pot. 3. Weigh the plants. 4. Spread the soil out to dry again, and dry the plants in the sun until they are crisp.
flow.say: Be very careful to keep every crumb of soil. If we lose soil, our test won't be fair.
flow.kid: Pull the plants out gently. Brush every crumb of soil back into the pot. Weigh the plants. Dry the soil again.
flow.wait: Let the plants and the soil dry for about a week.

flow.do: 1. Weigh the dried plants. 2. Weigh the dried soil in the same pot. 3. Compare the numbers.
flow.say: Our dry seeds weighed only a few grams. Now weigh the dry plants and the dry soil. What do you notice? So where did the plants come from?
flow.kid: Weigh the dry plants. Weigh the dry soil. Did the soil get lighter? Did the plants get heavier? Where did they come from?

check.q: The dry plants weighed more than the dry seeds. The soil weighed almost the same as at the start. Where did most of the plants come from?
check.why: The soil hardly changed, so the plants did not come from the soil. Dried plants have no water left in them. So most of what is left was built from carbon dioxide in the air, using sunlight. Picking 'the soil' is the old idea van Helmont tested. If plants ate soil, the soil would have got lighter. Your scale may show the soil 10 or 20 grams lighter or heavier. That is mostly damp left in the soil, or crumbs lost. A kitchen scale cannot measure a change as small as the plants' few grams. But it does show the soil did not lose a big amount.

chart.title: Van Helmont's willow tree, nearly 400 years ago (rounded to kilograms)
chart.note: The tree gained about 75 kilograms. The soil lost only about 60 grams, too little to show on this chart.

flow.parent: If the dry plants weigh less than the dry seeds, they did not get enough sun to make more food than they used. Try again in a sunnier place. The clearest result is the plants: they got only water, yet their dry weight grew. Dry the soil the same way both times, so its weight is as fair as possible.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: my plants were built mostly from air. What I saw: my 6 dry seeds weighed 4 grams, and the dried plants weighed 11 grams. The soil stayed at 1,200 grams. Why: the leaves used sunlight to build carbon dioxide from the air into sugar. The sugar became stems and leaves.

projects.context: In this five-week project, you weigh dry soil, grow plants in it with only water, and weigh everything again. It copies Jan Baptist van Helmont's famous willow experiment.

setup.caption: 1. Weigh the dry soil and the seeds. Then plant the seeds.

setup.art: The same pot a few weeks later with several tall bean plants, a ruler beside them, and a watering can of clean water.

challenges.title: Lunch on Mars
challenges.problem: Four astronauts will live on Mars for two years. Food and air from Earth will run out. Design a greenhouse that gives them food and helps make their air.
constraints: Mars air is very thin and mostly carbon dioxide. People cannot breathe it.
Mars gets less than half the sunlight Earth gets, and has big dust storms that can last for weeks.
There is ice under the ground, but no liquid water on top.
Everything must fit inside sealed rooms.
materials: a shoebox, cling film, a torch and cotton wool for a model, if you like
a seed packet, to choose crops
general: A sealed dome or room, with ordinary air inside for the plants and people.
Bright lamps, especially red and blue LED lights, to help on dark days and in dust storms.
Melt the ice and clean it, to water the plants.
Grow fast, filling crops like potatoes, beans, wheat and leafy greens.
creative: Pipe the astronauts' breath, full of carbon dioxide, into the greenhouse. Then pipe the plants' oxygen back.
Grow tiny green algae in tanks of water. They grow very fast and make a lot of oxygen.
Turn food scraps and plant waste into compost, so the minerals go round and round.
Grow plants in layers on shelves, like a tall cupboard, to save space.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own Mars greenhouse. Draw it and label every part. Show where the light, water and carbon dioxide come from, and where the food and oxygen go.

flow.do: Read the problem and the constraints together.
flow.say: A plant needs light, water and carbon dioxide to make food. Which of those does Mars have? Which are hard to get?
flow.kid: Read the problem. A plant needs light, water and carbon dioxide. Which does Mars have? Which are hard?
flow.context: This is the first step of Lunch on Mars, a design challenge. You plan a greenhouse where plants make food and air for astronauts.

flow.do: Make a list of three ideas before looking at any solutions.
flow.say: Engineers think before they build. Let's write three ideas of our own first.
flow.kid: Think like an engineer! Write or draw three ideas. Do this before you look at anyone else's.

check.q: Mars air is mostly carbon dioxide. Why is that good news for the plants?
options: Carbon dioxide is what leaves build sugar from
Carbon dioxide is a kind of water
Plants breathe it like we breathe oxygen, and need nothing else
check.why: Leaves take in carbon dioxide and build sugar from it, so Mars has plenty of one ingredient. Picking 'need nothing else' misses that plants also need light and water, and oxygen for their own respiration. The thin, cold Mars air also cannot keep a plant alive outside, which is why the greenhouse is sealed.

flow.do: 1. Draw the greenhouse and label each part. 2. Draw arrows for light, water and carbon dioxide going in. 3. Draw arrows for food and oxygen going to the astronauts.
flow.say: Show me where each ingredient comes from. What happens in a dust storm, when there is hardly any sunlight?
flow.kid: Draw your greenhouse. Label every part. Draw arrows for light, water and carbon dioxide going in. Where does the food go?
flow.parent: Good designs show a loop. People breathe out carbon dioxide for the plants. Plants give oxygen and food to the people. A strong design also has lamps for dust storms and a way to recycle waste.

flow.do: Read the usual and creative solutions together. Improve your design.
flow.say: Here are ideas that space scientists have really thought about. Can you add one to yours?
flow.kid: Look at the usual ideas and the creative ones. Can you make your design even better?
flow.think: On Earth, no one pipes our breath to the plants. How does the carbon dioxide we breathe out reach the leaves?

challenges.context: This is a design challenge. Astronauts on Mars need food and air. You design a greenhouse where plants make both by photosynthesis.

setup.art: A dusty red Martian landscape with a small sealed dome base and four astronauts in suits.
setup.caption: 1. Read the problem: four astronauts on Mars need food and air.

setup.art: A child drawing a greenhouse dome with shelves of plants, red and blue lamps, and arrows for light, water and air going in.
setup.caption: 2. Draw your greenhouse. Show light, water and carbon dioxide going in.

setup.art: A labelled drawing with a loop of arrows: astronauts breathing out carbon dioxide to plants, plants sending oxygen and food back.
setup.caption: 3. Show food and oxygen going to the astronauts.

challenges.title: The Fastest Float
challenges.problem: In the leaf disc experiment, the sunlit discs in baking soda water floated up after some minutes. Can you make 10 discs all float in less time?
constraints: You must use leaf discs cut with a straw, sunk in a syringe.
You may change only one thing at a time, so you know what made the difference.
Time each try with a clock.
materials: the leaf disc kit from the first experiment: spinach, a syringe, baking soda, washing-up liquid, cups
a desk lamp, warm water, and other kinds of leaves
general: Use brighter light: move the cup into strong sun, or bring a lamp closer.
Add a little more baking soda, for more carbon dioxide.
Use fresh, young, dark green leaves.
creative: Use slightly warm water, not hot. The chemical changes inside a leaf go faster when it is a little warm, up to a point.
Try leaves from different plants, like tulsi, coriander or a neem leaf, and see which is the fastest food maker.
Put the cup in front of a white sheet or a mirror to bounce more light onto it.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way to make the discs float faster. Test it. Remember to change only one thing.

flow.do: Find how long your sunlit discs took in the leaf disc experiment. Write it at the top of a page.
flow.say: Last time, how long did all 10 discs take to float? That's the time to beat.
flow.kid: How long did the discs take last time? Write that down. That is the time to beat!
flow.context: This is the first step of The Fastest Float. You try to make spinach leaf discs float up faster, by giving the leaf better conditions for making oxygen.

flow.do: List three ideas together before trying anything. For each idea, say which one thing will change.
flow.say: What could help the leaf make oxygen faster? For each idea, which one thing are we changing?
flow.kid: List three ideas to make the discs float faster. For each one, say the one thing you will change.

flow.do: 1. Try each idea, one at a time, with 10 fresh discs. 2. Time how long until all 10 float. 3. Write each time down.
flow.say: Try one idea at a time. If we change two things together, we won't know which one worked.
flow.kid: Try each idea one at a time. Time how long until all 10 float. Write each time down.

check.q: Kavya put her cup in brighter light AND added more baking soda at the same time. Her discs floated faster. What can she say?
options: Something helped, but she can't tell which change did it
check.why: She changed two things at once. So either one, or both together, might have made the difference. To find out, she must change only one thing at a time. Picking 'brighter light is the reason' is a good guess, but her test cannot prove it.

flow.parent: Brighter light and a little more baking soda usually help the most. Very hot water damages the leaf, so keep it only slightly warm. Some leaves, like thick waxy ones, are hard to sink in the syringe.

flow.do: Compare all the times. Read the usual and creative solutions together.
flow.say: Which change helped most? Here are some other ideas. Is there one you'd like to try?
flow.kid: Which change worked best? Look at the other ideas. Which would you try next?
flow.think: A field of rice is millions of leaves like these. How could a farmer help them make more food?

challenges.context: This is a challenge using the leaf disc experiment. You try to make sunk leaf discs float faster, by changing one thing at a time to help the leaf make oxygen.
