opts: How a leaf makes food from light, water and carbon dioxide
quiz.why: Photosynthesis means putting together with light. Picking 'drinks water' is close, because water is one ingredient. But photosynthesis is making food. Picking 'eats soil' is the most common wrong idea about plants.

quiz.p: Which gas comes OUT of a leaf while it makes food?
quiz.why: Oxygen is left over and goes out into the air. Picking 'carbon dioxide' mixes up in and out. Carbon dioxide goes into the leaf.

quiz.p: To test if a leaf needs light, which test is fair?
opts: Same leaf discs and same water, one cup in light and one in the dark
One cup in light with baking soda, one in the dark with plain water
Spinach in the light, tulsi in the dark
Ten discs in the light, two in the dark
quiz.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. Here that is the light. Picking the second answer changes two things at once, the light and the baking soda. Then you can't tell which one made the difference.
quiz.context: In the leaf disc experiment, sunk spinach discs float up when the leaf makes oxygen.

quiz.p: Look at the chart. Which cup made oxygen?
quiz.why: Only the cup with light and carbon dioxide made oxygen, so only its discs floated. Picking 'light and plain water' misses the carbon dioxide. Plain water has almost none.
quiz.context: In the leaf disc experiment, sunk spinach discs float up when the leaf makes oxygen.

chart.title: Made-up example: leaf discs floating after 15 minutes, out of 10
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what results can look like. Your numbers will be different.

quiz.p: Divya drops iodine on a slice of raw potato and on a spoon of sugar. The potato turns blue-black. The sugar stays brown. What does this show?
opts: The potato has starch in it, and the sugar does not
The sugar has more starch than the potato
Iodine only works on cold foods
Both have the same amount of starch
quiz.why: Iodine turns blue-black only on starch. Sugar is what leaves make first, and plants join sugars into starch to store them. So sugar itself stays brown. Picking 'sugar has more starch' mixes up the two.
quiz.context: In the starch test, you drop brown iodine on foods and watch for a blue-black colour.

quiz.p: A leaf with a paper star on it is tested with iodine. Where will it stay pale?
opts: Under the star, where no light fell
quiz.why: No light under the star means no food made there, so no starch. Picking 'everywhere except the star' has the answer backwards.
quiz.context: In the starch picture experiment, part of a leaf is covered with black paper for two sunny days, then tested for starch.

quiz.p: Most of a tree's dry weight came from where?
quiz.why: Leaves build the tree from carbon dioxide, with a little water. Picking 'sunlight' is close. Sunlight gives the energy, but the building blocks come from air. Picking 'the soil' is the oldest wrong idea.

quiz.p: Van Helmont's willow gained about 75 kilograms in five years. If the tree had been built from soil, what would he have found?
opts: The soil had lost about 75 kilograms
The soil weighed exactly the same
quiz.why: If the tree were built from soil, the soil would have lost as much as the tree gained. In fact it lost only about 60 grams. Picking 'exactly the same' is close to what he really saw, which is why it shows the tree was not built from soil.
quiz.context: Nearly 400 years ago, Jan Baptist van Helmont grew a willow in a weighed pot of soil for five years, giving it only rainwater.

opts: Leaves are green on the inside only
quiz.why: We see the colour that bounces back. Chlorophyll uses red and blue, and bounces green. Picking 'soaks up green' is the most common mix-up.

quiz.p: Moong sprouts grown in a dark cupboard are pale yellow. Why?
opts: Moong makes green chlorophyll only in light
They are a different kind of moong
quiz.why: Without light, the sprouts do not make green chlorophyll. Picking 'too cold' is a sensible guess about cupboards. But warm dark sprouts are pale too.

quiz.p: A potato is kept in a dark cupboard for a month. They grow long white shoots, and the potato gets lighter. Where did the food for the shoots come from?
opts: The starch stored in the potato, which they use up
quiz.why: In the dark, the potato cannot photosynthesise. So they live on the starch their leaves made last season. They use oxygen to get energy from it, and that is why they get lighter. Picking 'light in the cupboard' forgets that a dark cupboard has almost none.

quiz.p: A leopard eats a goat. Where did the leopard's energy first come from?
opts: The Sun, caught by the grass the goat ate
quiz.why: Energy passes along a food chain. It starts as sunlight caught by a plant. Picking 'the goat only' stops one step too soon.

quiz.p: Priestley's plants sometimes freshened the air in a jar and sometimes did not. In 1779, Jan Ingenhousz found what made the difference. What was it?
opts: Light: plants freshen air only in light, with their green parts
quiz.why: Ingenhousz did hundreds of tests in one summer. Plants gave out oxygen only in light, and only from their green parts. Picking 'the kind of soil' is the old idea that plants are made of soil.

quiz.p: Where did the oxygen in Earth's air first come from?
opts: Tiny cyanobacteria in the sea, over a very long time
quiz.why: Cyanobacteria made it by photosynthesis, long before trees existed. Picking 'the first trees' is a common guess. But trees came about 2 billion years later.

quiz.p: Is it fully known why leaves are green rather than black?
opts: No, there are several ideas and scientists still argue
quiz.why: It is still an open question. Picking 'yes, completely' is understandable, because chlorophyll's colour is well known. Why plants ended up with that colour is the puzzle.

applications: Farming: every crop, from rice and wheat to cotton and sugarcane, is a field of photosynthesis.
Greenhouses and polyhouses keep plants warm, and some farmers add extra carbon dioxide to make crops grow faster.
Grow lights with red and blue LEDs let people grow vegetables indoors, in cities and even on the International Space Station.
Fishponds and aquariums use water plants to add oxygen to the water.
Foresters measure how much carbon a forest stores by measuring its trees.
Satellites measure the green of land and sea to check on crops, forests and ocean life.
Plant breeders choose plants that give more food. In the 1930s, the Indian scientist Janaki Ammal helped breed sweeter sugarcane for India.
Scientists are trying to give rice the sugarcane way of catching carbon dioxide, so rice grows more grain.
Artificial leaves are being built to use sunlight to make clean fuels.
Coal, oil and gas are the remains of plants and tiny sea living things from millions of years ago. Burning them releases ancient stored sunlight and carbon.
Biogas plants in Indian villages turn cow dung and plant waste into cooking gas. That energy began as sunlight caught by grass.
Making jaggery and sugar from sugarcane collects sugar made by photosynthesis.

open_questions.q: Does quantum physics help leaves move light's energy so well?
open_questions.why_open: Experiments in 2007 suggested it might. Later experiments suggest the effect is too short to matter much. Scientists are still testing it.

open_questions.q: Why are plants green and not black?
open_questions.why_open: Several ideas compete, including the Purple Earth idea, keeping the energy supply steady, and protection from too much light. None is proved.

open_questions.q: How did the first living things learn to split water with light?
open_questions.why_open: The tiny metal cluster that splits water is very complicated. Nobody knows exactly how it first appeared, billions of years ago.

open_questions.q: Can we build an artificial leaf that is cheap and lasts?
open_questions.why_open: Some work in the lab, but they are expensive or wear out. A real leaf mends itself every day.

open_questions.q: Can rice be given the sugarcane trick for catching carbon dioxide?
open_questions.why_open: A big international project has worked on it since 2008. It needs many genes and leaf changes at once, and it is not done yet.

open_questions.q: How much extra carbon dioxide will forests and oceans soak up as there is more of it in the air?
open_questions.why_open: Plants grow faster with more carbon dioxide, but heat, drought and lack of minerals hold them back. Scientists disagree about how much.

open_questions.q: What colour would plants be on a planet with a different kind of star?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists, including Nancy Kiang at NASA, have worked out that plants around redder stars might look dark red or even black. Nobody has seen a plant on another planet yet.

maths.problem: In Build a Sugar, one carbon dioxide has 1 black ball and 2 red balls. One water has 2 white balls and 1 red ball. You built 6 of each. How many black, white and red balls did you use altogether?
maths.explain: 6 carbon dioxides, each with 1 black ball: 6 × 1 = 6 black. 6 waters, each with 2 white balls: 6 × 2 = 12 white. Red balls: 6 carbon dioxides × 2 = 12, and 6 waters × 1 = 6. 12 + 6 = 18 red. One sugar uses 6 black, 12 white and 6 red. So 18 − 6 = 12 red balls are left over. They make 6 pairs of oxygen.
maths.context: In Build a Sugar, you build models of carbon dioxide and water from clay balls. Black is carbon, red is oxygen and white is hydrogen. Then you rebuild them into sugar and oxygen.

maths.why_maths: A leaf cannot make or lose atoms. It can only rearrange them. Counting the balls in and out proves that every atom in the sugar came from the air and the water.

maths.problem: Look at the line chart from the leaf disc experiment. How many discs were floating at 9 minutes? How many more had floated up by 15 minutes?
maths.answer: 4 discs at 9 minutes. 6 more by 15 minutes.
maths.explain: Find 9 on the bottom line, go up to the line, and read across: 4 discs. At 15 minutes it reads 10. 10 − 4 = 6. So 6 more discs floated up in those 6 minutes.
maths.context: In the leaf disc experiment, tiny circles of spinach leaf are sunk in water. If the leaf makes oxygen, bubbles gather and the circles float back up.

maths.problem: Van Helmont's willow weighed about 2 kilograms at the start and about 77 kilograms after five years. How much weight did the willow gain? The soil lost only about 60 grams. Is that more or less than 1 kilogram?
maths.answer: The willow gained about 75 kilograms. 60 grams is much less than 1 kilogram.
maths.explain: 77 − 2 = 75. So the tree gained about 75 kilograms. 1 kilogram is 1,000 grams. 60 grams is much less than 1,000 grams. So the soil lost far less than 1 kilogram, while the tree gained 75 kilograms.
maths.context: Nearly 400 years ago, Jan Baptist van Helmont planted a small willow in a weighed pot of soil. He gave the willow only water for five years, then weighed everything again.

chart.title: Van Helmont's willow tree, nearly 400 years ago (rounded to kilograms)
chart.note: The tree gained about 75 kilograms. The soil lost only about 60 grams, too little to show on this chart.

maths.why_maths: Weighing is how van Helmont, and you, can prove where a tree came from. Comparing the tree's gain with the soil's loss shows the soil could not have been the source.

maths.problem: In the bubble count, the water plant gave 30 bubbles in a minute with the lamp 10 cm away. They gave 16 at 20 cm, and 6 at 40 cm. Draw a bar chart. How many more bubbles were there at 10 cm than at 40 cm?
maths.answer: 24 more bubbles. Here is the bar chart.
maths.explain: Draw one bar for each lamp distance, as tall as its number. The tallest bar is 10 cm, at 30. The shortest is 40 cm, at 6. 30 − 6 = 24. So there were 24 more bubbles a minute with the lamp close.
maths.context: In the bubble count, a water plant sits in a glass of water. They give off bubbles of oxygen as they make food. A lamp is put close by, far away, or switched off.

answer_chart.title: Made-up example: bubbles from a water plant in one minute
answer_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what results can look like. Your numbers will be different.

maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows at a glance that more light means more oxygen. Subtracting tells you exactly how much more.

maths.problem: In The Breath a Tree Eats, you learned that a grown-up breathes out about 1 kilogram of carbon dioxide each day. How much is that in one week? In 30 days?
maths.answer: 7 kilograms in a week. 30 kilograms in 30 days.
maths.explain: Each day adds 1 kilogram. A week has 7 days, so 7 × 1 = 7 kilograms. 30 days give 30 × 1 = 30 kilograms. That is about as heavy as a child of nine. Leaves around the world take in carbon dioxide like this all the time and build it into plants.
maths.context: In The Breath a Tree Eats, you blow into limewater and it turns milky. This shows your breath carries carbon dioxide, the gas leaves build sugar from.

answer_chart.title: Carbon dioxide one grown-up breathes out (about 1 kilogram a day)

maths.why_maths: An invisible gas is hard to imagine. Multiplying one day's breath into a month's shows how much carbon dioxide one person gives to the air, ready for leaves to use.

deep_truth.truth: Spinach leaf discs floated up only when they had both light and carbon dioxide. They were making food and oxygen from air and water, using light. how_we_found_out.story: For about 2,000 years, most people believed that plants eat soil. In the first half of the 1600s, Jan Baptist van Helmont, a doctor in what is now Belgium, tested this. He dried and weighed 200 pounds of soil, about 91 kilograms, and planted a willow that weighed about 2 kilograms. For five years he gave the tree only rainwater, and covered the pot so that dust could not fall in. The willow grew to about 77 kilograms. The soil had lost only about 60 grams. So the tree was not made of soil. Van Helmont decided that the willow was made of water. That was only partly right, because he did not know that air holds a gas plants can use. In 1771, Joseph Priestley in England found that a sprig of mint could make used-up air fit for a candle again. In 1779, Jan Ingenhousz showed that only the green parts of a plant do this, and only in light. In 1804, Nicolas-Théodore de Saussure weighed plants and the air around them with great care. He showed that plants gain weight by taking in carbon dioxide as well as water.
how_we_found_out.who: Jan Baptist van Helmont; Joseph Priestley; Jan Ingenhousz; Nicolas-Théodore de Saussure
how_we_found_out.when: The first half of the 1600s (the willow, published in 1648); 1771 (Priestley's mint); 1779 (Ingenhousz); 1804 (de Saussure)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Plants are made of the soil they grow in. Van Helmont's weighed pot showed that the soil hardly changed. His own idea, that the tree was made only of water, was shown wrong when de Saussure found that plants also build with carbon dioxide from the air.
